sections.title: Dynamic equilibrium: still outside, busy inside

board_events.text: Equilibrium is a balance of two rates
Picture a crowded Rajdhani coach at a busy platform.
As many people board as step off each minute, so the count inside stays constant.
Constant on the outside, furious two-way traffic on the inside.
This is dynamic equilibrium: nothing looks like it changes, yet both directions run at full speed.
Equilibrium is not a dead stop; it is two opposing rates that have become equal.

segments.text: <curious> Let me start with a picture you already know.
Imagine the Howrah to New Delhi Rajdhani standing at a packed platform in the morning rush.
Passengers keep boarding through some doors while others keep alighting through the rest, and if exactly as many board as leave each minute, the number inside the coach stays fixed.
To someone glancing from the platform nothing seems to move, but step inside and you see furious two-way traffic.
That is exactly what dynamic equilibrium means: the outside looks frozen, yet both directions are running hard.
The single condition that defines it is this: the forward rate has become equal to the reverse rate.
So never picture equilibrium as a reaction that has stopped; picture it as two opposing rates that have climbed and fallen until they match.
On this graph the forward rate starts high and falls, the reverse rate starts at zero and rises, and once they meet the concentrations stop changing.
<curious> चलिए एक जानी-पहचानी तस्वीर से शुरू करते हैं।
सोचिए Howrah से New Delhi वाली Rajdhani एक भरे हुए platform पर morning rush में खड़ी है।
कुछ doors से passengers चढ़ रहे हैं और बाकी से उतर रहे हैं, और अगर हर minute जितने चढ़ें उतने ही उतरें, तो coach के अंदर लोगों की count constant रहती है।
Platform से देखने पर कुछ बदलता नहीं दिखता, पर अंदर जाइए तो ज़बरदस्त two-way traffic चल रहा है।
यही dynamic equilibrium है: बाहर से सब स्थिर, पर अंदर दोनों directions पूरी रफ़्तार से चल रहे हैं।
इसे define करने वाली एक ही condition है: forward rate, reverse rate के बराबर हो जाती है।
इसलिए equilibrium को कभी रुकी हुई reaction मत समझिए; इसे दो opposite rates समझिए जो बढ़ते-घटते हुए बराबर हो गईं।
इस graph में forward rate ऊपर से गिरती है, reverse rate zero से उठती है, और जहाँ मिलती हैं वहाँ concentrations बदलना बंद कर देती हैं।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Physical equilibria all around us

board_events.text: Equilibrium shows up before any bond breaks
Seal a half-filled water bottle: evaporation and condensation balance out.
At 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere, ice melts as fast as water freezes.
Stir sugar into nimbu paani until no more dissolves: a saturated solution is an equilibrium.
Crack a sealed Thums-Up and the gas-dissolution balance breaks: fizz escapes.

segments.text: Equilibrium turns up long before any chemical bond breaks, in plain physical changes.

Seal a half-filled water bottle and leave it: water molecules keep escaping the surface while vapour molecules keep returning, until the two rates match and the vapour pressure locks to a fixed value.
We write that liquid water in equilibrium with its vapour.
The same balance governs melting: at zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere, ice melts at exactly the rate water freezes, so the slush sits there forever.
That is solid water in equilibrium with liquid water.

Keep stirring sugar into a glass of nimbu paani and eventually no more dissolves; that saturated solution is a genuine equilibrium, with crystals dissolving as fast as dissolved sugar re-crystallises.
We write solid sugar in equilibrium with dissolved sugar.
And the fizz trapped in a sealed Thums-Up is dissolved gas at equilibrium under pressure; crack the cap, the pressure drops, the balance breaks, and the gas rushes out.
Equilibrium किसी chemical bond के टूटने से बहुत पहले, simple physical changes में ही दिख जाता है।
आधी भरी water bottle seal करके छोड़ दीजिए: surface से molecules उड़ते रहते हैं और vapour वापस लौटता रहता है, जब तक दोनों rates बराबर होकर vapour pressure एक fixed value पर lock न हो जाए।
इसे हम liquid water का अपने vapour के साथ equilibrium लिखते हैं।
यही balance melting में है: zero degree Celsius और one atmosphere पर बर्फ उतनी ही तेज़ी से पिघलती है जितनी तेज़ी से पानी जमता है, इसलिए slush वहीं टिका रहता है।
यह solid water का liquid water के साथ equilibrium है।
नींबू पानी में sugar घोलते जाइए, एक point पर और नहीं घुलेगी; वो saturated solution एक असली equilibrium है, जहाँ crystals उतनी तेज़ी से घुल रहे हैं जितनी तेज़ी से वापस बन रहे हैं।
इसे solid sugar का dissolved sugar के साथ equilibrium लिखते हैं।
और sealed Thums-Up की fizz pressure के नीचे dissolved gas का equilibrium है; cap खोलिए, pressure गिरता है, balance टूटता है, और gas बाहर निकल भागती है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Reversible reactions reach one destination

board_events.text: Same equilibrium, whichever gate you enter
Seal hydrogen and iodine vapour: they form HI, and HI breaks back apart, both at once.
A reversible reaction in a closed system always settles into equilibrium.
Start from pure reactants or pure product: you land on the SAME mixture.
How FAR a reaction goes is set by K; how FAST it gets there is a separate kinetics question.
A large K means near-complete reaction, saying nothing about microseconds versus millennia.

segments.text: Now let the molecules actually react, and the same balance appears chemically.
Seal hydrogen and iodine vapour together: they combine to give hydrogen iodide, and at the same time hydrogen iodide breaks back into its elements, both reactions running together.
We write hydrogen plus iodine in equilibrium with two hydrogen iodide.
A reaction that can go both ways and never fully finishes in a closed vessel is reversible, and a reversible reaction in a closed system always settles into equilibrium.
Here is the beautiful experimental fact: you reach the identical equilibrium mixture whether you start with pure hydrogen and iodine or with pure hydrogen iodide.
<curious> And keep two ideas apart: how far a reaction ends up going is set by the equilibrium constant, while how fast it arrives is a completely separate kinetics question.
A large equilibrium constant tells you the reaction goes almost to completion, but it says nothing about whether that takes a microsecond or a millennium.
अब molecules को सच में react करने दीजिए, वही balance chemically दिखता है।
Hydrogen और iodine vapour को seal कर दीजिए: ये मिलकर hydrogen iodide बनाते हैं, और साथ-साथ hydrogen iodide वापस टूटता भी है, दोनों reactions एक साथ चलती हैं।
इसे hydrogen plus iodine का two hydrogen iodide के साथ equilibrium लिखते हैं।
जो reaction दोनों तरफ़ जा सके और closed vessel में कभी पूरी न हो, वो reversible है, और closed system में reversible reaction हमेशा equilibrium पर आ जाती है।
यहाँ एक बहुत सुंदर experimental fact है: आप चाहे pure hydrogen और iodine से शुरू करें या pure hydrogen iodide से, आप बिलकुल एक ही equilibrium mixture पर पहुँचते हैं।
<curious> और दो बातें अलग रखिए: reaction कितनी दूर जाएगी यह equilibrium constant तय करता है, जबकि कितनी जल्दी पहुँचेगी यह बिलकुल अलग kinetics का सवाल है।
बड़ा equilibrium constant बताता है कि reaction लगभग पूरी होती है, पर यह नहीं बताता कि इसमें एक microsecond लगेगा या एक millennium।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: The conditions equilibrium needs

board_events.text: When can equilibrium even exist?
Closed system: open the flask and products escape, so equilibrium never establishes.
The train coach must keep its doors AND its walls.
Constant temperature: K is a constant only at fixed T; change T and you get a different K.
No bulk disturbance: equilibrium is reached spontaneously and holds only while nothing is added or removed.
Ideal behaviour: the clean constant-ratio law assumes dilute solutions and ideal gases.
Real high-pressure or concentrated systems need activities, not raw concentrations.

segments.text: Equilibrium only appears when a few conditions are met, so let us list them.
First, the system must be closed: open the flask and let products escape, and equilibrium can never establish, because one direction is always draining away.
The train-coach picture only works if the coach keeps both its doors and its walls.
Second, temperature must be constant, because the equilibrium constant is a constant only at a fixed temperature; change the temperature and you get a genuinely different value of K.
Third, there must be no bulk disturbance: equilibrium is reached spontaneously and stays put only while nothing is being added or removed from outside.
Fourth, the neat constant-ratio law we are about to write assumes the species behave ideally, meaning dilute solutions and ideal gases.
Real systems at high pressure or high concentration need activities rather than raw concentrations, a refinement you meet later.
Equilibrium तभी आता है जब कुछ conditions पूरी हों, तो चलिए उन्हें list करते हैं।
पहली, system closed होना चाहिए: flask खोलकर products को निकलने दीजिए तो equilibrium कभी नहीं बनेगा, क्योंकि एक direction लगातार खाली होती रहती है।
Train-coach वाली तस्वीर तभी चलती है जब coach के doors और walls दोनों बने रहें।
दूसरी, temperature constant होना चाहिए, क्योंकि equilibrium constant सिर्फ़ fixed temperature पर ही constant है; temperature बदलिए तो K की सचमुच अलग value मिलती है।
तीसरी, कोई bulk disturbance नहीं होनी चाहिए: equilibrium अपने-आप बनता है और तभी टिकता है जब बाहर से कुछ add या remove न हो।
चौथी, जो neat constant-ratio law हम अभी लिखेंगे वो मानता है कि species ideally behave करें, यानी dilute solutions और ideal gases।
High pressure या high concentration वाले real systems को raw concentrations की जगह activities चाहिए, जो एक बाद में आने वाला refinement है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Heterogeneous equilibria: the pure-phase rule

board_events.text: Pure solids and liquids drop out of K
When more than one phase is present, the equilibrium is heterogeneous.
A pure solid or pure liquid has a concentration fixed by its density, independent of amount.
So it is folded into the constant and OMITTED from the expression.
Both solids vanish; the constant depends only on the pressure of carbon dioxide.
Writing bracket CaO or bracket CaCO3 is the single most penalised error in Boards.

segments.text: When more than one phase is present the equilibrium is called heterogeneous, and it hides a very useful simplification.
The active mass of a pure solid or a pure liquid is its molar concentration, and that is fixed by its density.
Crucially, that value does not depend on how much of the solid or liquid you have sitting there.
Because it is a fixed number, it gets absorbed into the equilibrium constant and is simply left out of the written expression.
Take the thermal decomposition of limestone: solid calcium carbonate in equilibrium with solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas.
Both solids disappear from the expression, leaving the constant equal to just the partial pressure of carbon dioxide.
So the whole equilibrium is governed by one gas pressure, no matter how big the lump of limestone is.
<whisper> And a warning: writing a concentration term for calcium oxide or calcium carbonate is the single most penalised mistake in Board exams.
जब एक से ज़्यादा phase मौजूद हों तो equilibrium heterogeneous कहलाता है, और इसमें एक बहुत काम का simplification छुपा है।
किसी pure solid या pure liquid का active mass उसका molar concentration है, और वो उसकी density से तय होता है।
सबसे ख़ास बात, वो value इस बात पर निर्भर नहीं करती कि आपके पास कितना solid या liquid रखा है।
चूँकि यह एक fixed number है, इसे equilibrium constant में समेट लिया जाता है और expression से हटा दिया जाता है।
Limestone के thermal decomposition को लीजिए: solid calcium carbonate का solid calcium oxide और carbon dioxide gas के साथ equilibrium।
दोनों solids expression से ग़ायब हो जाते हैं, और constant सिर्फ़ carbon dioxide के partial pressure के बराबर रह जाता है।
तो पूरा equilibrium एक ही gas pressure से चलता है, चाहे limestone का टुकड़ा कितना भी बड़ा हो।
<whisper> और एक चेतावनी: calcium oxide या calcium carbonate का concentration term लिखना Board exams की सबसे ज़्यादा marks कटवाने वाली ग़लती है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Sizing up a reaction: K for extent, Q for direction

board_events.text: Read K for how far, read Q for which way
The magnitude of K tells you how far a reaction goes.
$K_c \gt 10^{3}$: products dominate, reaction nearly complete.
$K_c \lt 10^{-3}$: reactants dominate, reaction barely proceeds.
Between those, appreciable amounts of both sit at equilibrium.
The reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but is evaluated at any instant, not just equilibrium.
$Q \lt K$: too few products, run forward. $Q \gt K$: too many, run backward.
When Q equals K, the system is already at equilibrium and there is no net change.

segments.text: Two quick reads let you judge a reaction at a glance: its extent and its direction.
First, the sheer size of the equilibrium constant tells you how far a reaction goes.
If K c is greater than ten to the power three, products dominate and the reaction is nearly complete.
If K c is less than ten to the power minus three, reactants dominate and the reaction barely proceeds.
In between those limits you find appreciable amounts of both reactants and products sitting together at equilibrium.
Now for direction, use the reaction quotient Q: it has exactly the same algebraic form as K, but you evaluate it at any arbitrary instant, not necessarily at equilibrium.
Compare the two: if Q is less than K there are too few products so the reaction runs forward, and if Q is greater than K there are too many products so it runs backward.
And when Q equals K, the system is already sitting at equilibrium, so there is no net change at all.
दो quick reads से आप reaction को एक नज़र में परख सकते हैं: उसका extent और उसकी direction।
पहला, equilibrium constant का साइज़ बताता है कि reaction कितनी दूर जाती है।
अगर K c, ten to the power three से बड़ा है, तो products हावी हैं और reaction लगभग पूरी है।
अगर K c, ten to the power minus three से छोटा है, तो reactants हावी हैं और reaction मुश्किल से आगे बढ़ती है।
इन दोनों limits के बीच में reactants और products दोनों की appreciable मात्रा equilibrium पर साथ रहती है।
अब direction के लिए reaction quotient Q इस्तेमाल कीजिए: इसका algebraic form बिलकुल K जैसा है, पर आप इसे किसी भी instant पर निकालते हैं, ज़रूरी नहीं equilibrium पर।
दोनों की तुलना कीजिए: अगर Q, K से छोटा है तो products कम हैं इसलिए reaction forward चलती है, और अगर Q, K से बड़ा है तो products ज़्यादा हैं इसलिए backward चलती है।
और जब Q बराबर K हो, तो system पहले से ही equilibrium पर है, इसलिए कोई net change नहीं होता।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Law of mass action: writing Kc and Kp

board_events.text: The constant-ratio law
For a reversible reaction with stoichiometric coefficients a, b, c, d:
Concentration constant: products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
For gases, the same ratio built from equilibrium partial pressures gives K p.
Each bracket is an equilibrium molar concentration in mol per litre.

segments.text: The law of mass action turns the balance of rates into a clean algebraic law.
Take a general reversible reaction with stoichiometric coefficients a, b, c and d.
We write it as a A plus b B in equilibrium with c C plus d D.
The concentration equilibrium constant is the product concentrations on top and the reactant concentrations on the bottom, each raised to its own stoichiometric coefficient.
So K c equals bracket C to the power c times bracket D to the power d, all divided by bracket A to the power a times bracket B to the power b.
For a gaseous equilibrium we build exactly the same ratio, but from the equilibrium partial pressures, and call it K p.
So K p equals p C to the power c times p D to the power d, over p A to the power a times p B to the power b.
And remember every square bracket here is an equilibrium molar concentration, measured in moles per litre.
Law of mass action rates के balance को एक साफ़ algebraic law में बदल देता है।
एक general reversible reaction लीजिए जिसके stoichiometric coefficients a, b, c और d हैं।
इसे हम a A plus b B का c C plus d D के साथ equilibrium लिखते हैं।
Concentration equilibrium constant में ऊपर products के concentrations और नीचे reactants के concentrations आते हैं, हर एक अपने stoichiometric coefficient की power पर।
तो K c बराबर bracket C to the power c into bracket D to the power d, divided by bracket A to the power a into bracket B to the power b।
Gaseous equilibrium के लिए हम बिलकुल यही ratio बनाते हैं, पर equilibrium partial pressures से, और उसे K p कहते हैं।
तो K p बराबर p C to the power c into p D to the power d, over p A to the power a into p B to the power b।
और याद रखिए, यहाँ हर square bracket एक equilibrium molar concentration है, moles per litre में।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: The Kp–Kc bridge, and the units of K

board_events.text: Converting the currency: concentration to pressure
For any gas, the ideal-gas law gives partial pressure as concentration times R T.
Substitute into K p and the leftover power of R T is exactly delta n:

board_events.latex: K_p = K_c\,(RT)^{\Delta n}, \quad \Delta n = n_{\text{gas,prod}} - n_{\text{gas,react}}

board_events.text: Only gaseous species count in delta n; solids and liquids are excluded.
K has no fixed dimension; its units track delta n.
When $\Delta n = 0$, K is dimensionless and $K_p = K_c$.

segments.text: The bridge between K p and K c is just a change of currency, from concentration to pressure.
For any gaseous species, the ideal-gas law says pressure times volume equals moles times R T.
Rearranged, the partial pressure of species i equals its moles over volume times R T, which is simply its concentration times R T.
Substitute that pressure-equals-concentration-times-R-T into every term of the K p expression, and the concentration parts rebuild K c while the R T factors collect together.
The leftover power of R T is precisely delta n, giving K p equals K c times R T raised to the power delta n, where delta n is gaseous product moles minus gaseous reactant moles.
<excited> And watch this: only gaseous species count in delta n, so solids and liquids are simply not counted.
Because delta n can be positive, negative or zero, the equilibrium constant has no fixed dimension; its units track delta n.
So the units of K c are moles per litre raised to delta n, and the units of K p are atmospheres raised to delta n.
And in the special case where delta n is zero, K is dimensionless and K p equals K c outright, with no conversion cost at all.
K p और K c के बीच का bridge बस currency बदलने जैसा है, concentration से pressure में।
किसी भी gaseous species के लिए ideal-gas law कहता है pressure into volume बराबर moles into R T।
Rearrange करने पर species i का partial pressure बराबर उसके moles over volume into R T, जो सीधे उसका concentration into R T है।
इस pressure-equals-concentration-into-R-T को K p के हर term में रखिए, तो concentration वाले हिस्से फिर से K c बना देते हैं और R T वाले factors इकट्ठे हो जाते हैं।
बचा हुआ R T का power ठीक delta n होता है, जिससे मिलता है K p बराबर K c into R T raised to the power delta n, जहाँ delta n है gaseous product moles minus gaseous reactant moles।
<excited> और यह देखिए: delta n में सिर्फ़ gaseous species गिने जाते हैं, इसलिए solids और liquids बिलकुल नहीं गिने जाते।
चूँकि delta n positive, negative या zero हो सकता है, equilibrium constant का कोई fixed dimension नहीं है; इसके units delta n के हिसाब से चलते हैं।
तो K c के units हैं moles per litre raised to delta n, और K p के units हैं atmospheres raised to delta n।
और उस ख़ास case में जहाँ delta n zero है, K dimensionless है और K p सीधे K c के बराबर, बिना किसी conversion cost के।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: The four-rule toolkit for combining equilibria

board_events.text: Reverse inverts, multiply powers, add multiplies
Reverse the reaction and you invert the constant.
Multiply every coefficient by n and you raise the constant to the power n.
Add two reactions and you multiply their constants.
The intermediate cancels on adding: that is why constants multiply.

segments.text: These four rules follow straight from the definition of K, and they power every combine-reaction problem.
Rule one: reverse the reaction, and you invert the constant.
So the reversed reaction has a constant equal to one over K.
Rule two and three come as a pair: multiply every stoichiometric coefficient by n and you raise the whole constant to the power n.
So scaling up by n gives K to the power n, and dividing by n gives the n-th root, K to the power one over n.
Rule four: add two reactions together, and you multiply their constants.
So the net constant equals K one times K two.
The reason is clean: K is a ratio of concentration terms with stoichiometric exponents, and when you add mechanisms the intermediate cancels, so the two ratios simply multiply.
ये चार rules सीधे K की definition से निकलते हैं, और ये हर combine-reaction problem को चलाते हैं।
Rule one: reaction को reverse कीजिए, तो constant invert हो जाता है।
यानी reversed reaction का constant बराबर one over K।
Rule two और three एक जोड़ी में आते हैं: हर stoichiometric coefficient को n से multiply कीजिए तो पूरा constant n की power पर चढ़ जाता है।
तो n से scale up करने पर K to the power n, और n से divide करने पर n-th root, यानी K to the power one over n।
Rule four: दो reactions को जोड़िए, तो उनके constants multiply होते हैं।
यानी net constant बराबर K one into K two।
वजह साफ़ है: K, stoichiometric exponents वाले concentration terms का ratio है, और जब आप mechanisms जोड़ते हैं तो intermediate cancel हो जाता है, इसलिए दोनों ratios बस multiply हो जाते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Worked example — Kc from an equilibrium mixture (CBSE)

board_events.text: Find Kc with units for ammonia synthesis
A 2 L vessel at equilibrium holds 1.0 mol N2, 2.0 mol H2 and 0.80 mol NH3.
First convert moles to molar concentrations by dividing by the 2 L volume.
Here delta n is 2 minus 4, which is minus 2, so units are moles per litre to the minus two.

segments.text: Here is a clean Board-level calculation of an equilibrium constant with its units.
A two litre sealed vessel at equilibrium holds one point zero mole of nitrogen, two point zero moles of hydrogen, and zero point eight zero mole of ammonia.
The reaction is nitrogen plus three hydrogen in equilibrium with two ammonia.
The very first step is to turn moles into molar concentrations by dividing each amount by the two litre volume.
That gives nitrogen at zero point five zero molar, hydrogen at one point zero molar, and ammonia at zero point four zero molar.
Now substitute: K c equals ammonia squared over nitrogen times hydrogen cubed, which is zero point four zero squared over zero point five zero times one point zero cubed, giving zero point three two.
For the units, delta n is two minus four, that is minus two, so the constant carries units of moles per litre raised to the minus two.
So the final answer is K c equals zero point three two, in units of mole to the minus two litre squared.
यह equilibrium constant का एक साफ़-सुथरा Board-level calculation है, units के साथ।
एक two litre sealed vessel में equilibrium पर है one point zero mole nitrogen, two point zero moles hydrogen, और zero point eight zero mole ammonia।
Reaction है nitrogen plus three hydrogen का two ammonia के साथ equilibrium।
सबसे पहला step है moles को molar concentrations में बदलना, हर मात्रा को two litre volume से divide करके।
इससे मिलता है nitrogen zero point five zero molar, hydrogen one point zero molar, और ammonia zero point four zero molar।

अब substitute कीजिए: K c बराबर ammonia squared over nitrogen into hydrogen cubed, यानी zero point four zero squared over zero point five zero into one point zero cubed, जो देता है zero point three two।
Units के लिए delta n है two minus four, यानी minus two, इसलिए constant के units हैं moles per litre raised to minus two।
तो final answer है K c बराबर zero point three two, units में mole to the minus two litre squared।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Worked example — the Δn = 0 shortcut (NEET speed trap)

board_events.text: State Kp without a calculator
At 717 K, Kc equals 49 for hydrogen plus iodine forming hydrogen iodide.
The trap: a panicking student starts multiplying $0.0821 \times 717$.
Stop and read delta n first: two moles of gas on each side.
Every Kp–Kc question: glance at delta n before touching the calculator.

segments.text: This is a classic N E E T speed trap, and the whole point is to not calculate.
At seven hundred seventeen kelvin, K c equals forty nine for hydrogen plus iodine in equilibrium with two hydrogen iodide.
So we are given hydrogen plus iodine forming hydrogen iodide with K c equal to forty nine.
The trap is that a panicking student immediately reaches for K p equals K c times R T to the delta n, and starts multiplying zero point zero eight two one by seven hundred seventeen.
<chuckle> Stop, and read delta n first: there are two moles of gas on the left and two moles of gas on the right.
So delta n is two minus two, which is zero, and R T raised to the power zero is simply one.
Therefore K p equals K c equals forty nine, with no arithmetic needed at all.
The lesson is permanent: every time a K p versus K c question appears, glance at delta n before you touch the calculator.
यह एक classic N E E T speed trap है, और पूरी बात यही है कि calculate मत कीजिए।
Seven hundred seventeen kelvin पर K c बराबर forty nine है, hydrogen plus iodine के two hydrogen iodide के साथ equilibrium के लिए।
तो हमें दिया है hydrogen plus iodine से hydrogen iodide बनना, K c बराबर forty nine के साथ।
Trap यह है कि घबराया हुआ student तुरंत K p equals K c into R T to the delta n पकड़ लेता है, और zero point zero eight two one को seven hundred seventeen से multiply करने लगता है।
<chuckle> रुकिए, और पहले delta n पढ़िए: बाईं तरफ़ two moles gas और दाईं तरफ़ भी two moles gas।
तो delta n है two minus two, यानी zero, और R T raised to the power zero बस one होता है।
इसलिए K p बराबर K c बराबर forty nine, बिना किसी arithmetic के।
सबक़ पक्का है: जब भी K p versus K c का सवाल आए, calculator छूने से पहले delta n पर एक नज़र डालिए।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Worked example — PCl5 dissociation, Kp in α and P (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Derive Kp for a single-reactant dissociation
Start with 1 mol PCl5; at dissociation alpha the equilibrium moles are 1 minus alpha, alpha, alpha.
Total moles are 1 plus alpha, and each partial pressure is its mole fraction times P.
Now plug in alpha equals 0.50 and P equals 1.5 atmospheres.
Memorise this alpha-squared-P over one-minus-alpha-squared form; it recurs everywhere.

segments.text: This J E E Main favourite builds a reusable formula for any single-reactant dissociation.
Phosphorus pentachloride gas dissociates into phosphorus trichloride gas plus chlorine gas.
Start with one mole of phosphorus pentachloride, and let the degree of dissociation be alpha, so the equilibrium moles are one minus alpha, alpha, and alpha.
The total number of moles is therefore one plus alpha, and each partial pressure is that species' mole fraction times the total pressure P.
Feeding those in, K p equals the product of the two product pressures over the reactant pressure, which simplifies beautifully to alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared.
Now put in the numbers: alpha equals zero point five zero and P equals one point five atmospheres.
That gives zero point five zero squared times one point five, over one minus zero point five zero squared, which is zero point three seven five over zero point seven five.
So K p equals zero point five zero atmosphere; and do memorise this alpha-squared-P over one-minus-alpha-squared form, because it returns for every single-reactant to two-gas dissociation.
यह J E E Main का पसंदीदा सवाल किसी भी single-reactant dissociation के लिए एक reusable formula बनाता है।
Phosphorus pentachloride gas टूटकर phosphorus trichloride gas plus chlorine gas बनाती है।
One mole phosphorus pentachloride से शुरू कीजिए, और degree of dissociation को alpha मानिए, तो equilibrium moles हैं one minus alpha, alpha, और alpha।
इसलिए total moles हैं one plus alpha, और हर partial pressure उस species के mole fraction into total pressure P के बराबर है।
इन्हें डालने पर K p बराबर दोनों product pressures का गुणा over reactant pressure, जो ख़ूबसूरती से simplify होकर alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared बन जाता है।
अब numbers रखिए: alpha बराबर zero point five zero और P बराबर one point five atmospheres।
इससे मिलता है zero point five zero squared into one point five, over one minus zero point five zero squared, यानी zero point three seven five over zero point seven five।
तो K p बराबर zero point five zero atmosphere; और इस alpha-squared-P over one-minus-alpha-squared form को ज़रूर याद रखिए, क्योंकि हर single-reactant से two-gas dissociation में यह लौटकर आता है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Worked example — stacking equilibria with the toolkit (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Build the target reaction from two given ones
Given reaction one: carbon plus carbon dioxide forming two carbon monoxide, K1 equals 0.50.
Given reaction two: phosgene forming carbon monoxide plus chlorine, K2 equals 0.10.
Target: carbon plus carbon dioxide plus two chlorine forming two phosgene.
Reverse reaction two and use it twice, then add to reaction one.
The 2 CO intermediate cancels, and pure solid carbon never enters any expression.

segments.text: This Advanced problem is pure toolkit: stack the given reactions to build the target.
Reaction one is solid carbon plus carbon dioxide in equilibrium with two carbon monoxide, with K one equal to zero point five zero.
Reaction two is phosgene in equilibrium with carbon monoxide plus chlorine, with K two equal to zero point one zero.
The target we want is solid carbon plus carbon dioxide plus two chlorine in equilibrium with two phosgene.
Since we need two phosgene as a product, reverse reaction two, which inverts its constant, and use it twice, which squares that inverted constant, then add the result to reaction one.
Multiplying the constants gives K equals K one times one over K two, all squared, which is K one over K two squared.
Putting in the numbers, that is zero point five zero over zero point one zero squared, which is zero point five zero over zero point zero one, equal to fifty.
Notice the two carbon monoxide intermediate cancels on adding, which is exactly why adding reactions multiplies constants, and the pure solid carbon never enters any expression.
यह Advanced problem शुद्ध toolkit है: दी गई reactions को stack करके target बनाइए।
Reaction one है solid carbon plus carbon dioxide का two carbon monoxide के साथ equilibrium, K one बराबर zero point five zero के साथ।
Reaction two है phosgene का carbon monoxide plus chlorine के साथ equilibrium, K two बराबर zero point one zero के साथ।
जो target हमें चाहिए वो है solid carbon plus carbon dioxide plus two chlorine का two phosgene के साथ equilibrium।

चूँकि हमें product में two phosgene चाहिए, reaction two को reverse कीजिए, जिससे constant invert होता है, और इसे दो बार इस्तेमाल कीजिए, जिससे वो inverted constant square होता है, फिर result को reaction one में जोड़िए।
Constants को multiply करने पर मिलता है K बराबर K one into one over K two, whole squared, यानी K one over K two squared।
Numbers रखने पर वो है zero point five zero over zero point one zero squared, यानी zero point five zero over zero point zero one, बराबर fifty।
ध्यान दीजिए, जोड़ने पर two carbon monoxide intermediate cancel हो जाता है, यही वजह है कि reactions जोड़ने पर constants multiply होते हैं, और pure solid carbon किसी expression में नहीं आता।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Equilibrium — Kc and Kp
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for Kc and Kp

board_events.text: The four errors that cost the most marks
Never put pure solids or liquids into the K expression.
Only temperature changes K; pressure, concentration, inert gas and catalyst do not.
Delta n uses gaseous moles only, so solids and liquids never count.
Anchor the direction logic once: Q too big means go backward, Q too small means go forward.
Before any Kp–Kc numeric, compute delta n in your head first.
If $\Delta n = 0$, just write $K_p = K_c$ and move on.
For dissociation problems, reuse the ready-made alpha-squared-P over one-minus-alpha-squared result.

segments.text: Let us lock in the four mistakes that quietly drain marks in this subtopic.
First, never put a pure solid or a pure liquid into the equilibrium expression; their activities are fixed and already folded into K.
Second, remember that only temperature changes the value of K, while pressure, concentration, adding an inert gas, and a catalyst all leave it untouched.
Third, delta n counts gaseous moles only, so any solid or liquid in the equation is simply ignored when you compute it.
Fourth, anchor the direction rule once and for all: if Q is too big there are excess products so go backward, and if Q is too small go forward.
Now two pro-tips. Before any K p versus K c calculation, work out delta n in your head first.
<whisper> If delta n turns out to be zero, just write K p equals K c and move straight on, saving all the R T arithmetic.
And for dissociation problems, reuse the ready-made result, K p equals alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared, instead of rebuilding the whole table every time.
चलिए इस subtopic में चुपचाप marks खाने वाली चार ग़लतियाँ पक्की कर लेते हैं।
पहली, pure solid या pure liquid को कभी equilibrium expression में मत डालिए; उनकी activities fixed हैं और पहले ही K में समा चुकी हैं।
दूसरी, याद रखिए सिर्फ़ temperature K की value बदलता है, जबकि pressure, concentration, inert gas डालना, और catalyst सब इसे नहीं छूते।
तीसरी, delta n सिर्फ़ gaseous moles गिनता है, इसलिए equation में कोई भी solid या liquid इसे निकालते वक़्त नज़रअंदाज़ हो जाता है।
चौथी, direction rule एक बार में पक्का कर लीजिए: अगर Q बहुत बड़ा है तो products ज़्यादा हैं इसलिए backward जाइए, और अगर Q बहुत छोटा है तो forward जाइए।
अब दो pro-tips। किसी भी K p versus K c calculation से पहले delta n दिमाग़ में निकाल लीजिए।
<whisper> अगर delta n zero निकले, तो बस K p equals K c लिखकर आगे बढ़ जाइए, सारा R T का arithmetic बच जाता है।
और dissociation problems में हर बार पूरी table बनाने की जगह ready-made result दोबारा इस्तेमाल कीजिए, K p equals alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Why equilibrium stops where it does: the Gibbs valley

board_events.text: A reaction rolls downhill in Gibbs energy
Sub-01 told us where a reaction stops and which way it moves; now, why does it stop at all?
A reaction runs in whatever direction lowers the system's Gibbs energy G, and halts when G can fall no further.

board_events.text: Picture the mixture as a ball on a curved landscape: height is Gibbs energy, position is how far the reaction has gone.
The ball settles at the lowest point, not at pure reactants or pure products.
A large negative standard Gibbs change puts the valley far right, so products dominate and K is huge.

segments.text: The previous subtopic told us where a reaction stops and which way it moves, but now we answer the deeper question: why does it stop there at all?
The answer is the most important idea in chemical thermodynamics.
A reaction runs in whatever direction lowers the system's Gibbs energy, and it halts precisely when the Gibbs energy can fall no further.
Picture it on this landscape, where height is Gibbs energy and the horizontal position is how far the reaction has gone, from all reactants on the left to all products on the right.
<curious> The mixture behaves like a ball on that curve, and it always rolls downhill.
But it does not stop at the far right or the far left; it settles at the lowest point of the valley, somewhere in between.
At that valley floor the ground is flat, so the slope is zero, which means the Gibbs change delta G is zero.
And the position of the floor is set by the standard Gibbs change: a large negative value puts the valley far to the right, so products dominate and K is huge.
पिछले subtopic ने बताया कि reaction कहाँ रुकती है और किस तरफ़ जाती है, पर अब हम गहरा सवाल पूछते हैं: वो वहीं क्यों रुकती है?
इसका जवाब chemical thermodynamics का सबसे अहम idea है।
Reaction उसी direction में चलती है जो system की Gibbs energy घटाए, और ठीक तब रुकती है जब Gibbs energy और नीचे न गिर सके।
इसे इस landscape पर देखिए, जहाँ height है Gibbs energy और horizontal position है reaction कितनी दूर गई, बाईं तरफ़ all reactants से दाईं तरफ़ all products तक।
<curious> Mixture इस curve पर एक ball की तरह behave करता है, और हमेशा नीचे की ओर लुढ़कता है।
पर वो न बिलकुल दाएँ रुकता है न बिलकुल बाएँ; वो valley के सबसे नीचे वाले point पर, कहीं बीच में जाकर बैठता है।
उस valley floor पर ज़मीन flat है, इसलिए slope zero है, यानी Gibbs change delta G zero है।
और floor की position standard Gibbs change तय करता है: बड़ी negative value valley को दाईं तरफ़ ले जाती है, तो products हावी होते हैं और K बहुत बड़ा होता है।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: ΔG versus ΔG°: the slope now vs the fixed landscape

board_events.text: Two quantities you must never blur
Delta G with no degree sign is the slope of the landscape at the current composition.
$\Delta G \lt 0$ forward; $\Delta G \gt 0$ backward; $\Delta G = 0$ at the bottom.
Delta G standard, with the degree sign, is a fixed number for the reaction at a given temperature.
It is the Gibbs change with everything in its standard state, and it locates the valley and fixes K.
Only delta G standard goes into the minus R T ln K relation.
A large negative standard value gives K greater than one; a large positive value gives K much less than one.
So delta G standard and K are simply two ways of saying the same thing.

segments.text: Two Gibbs quantities look almost identical on paper, and exams punish students who blur them, so let us separate them cleanly.
Delta G, written with no degree sign, is the slope of the landscape at the current composition.
Its sign tells you which way the ball rolls right now: negative means forward, positive means backward, and zero means you are at the bottom, at equilibrium.
Delta G standard, written with the little degree sign, is something quite different: it is a single fixed number for the reaction at a given temperature.
It is the Gibbs change when everything sits in its standard state, and its job is to locate the valley and fix the value of K.
This distinction matters because only delta G standard, never the plain delta G, goes into the minus R T ln K relation.
A large negative standard value gives K greater than one, and a large positive standard value gives K much less than one.
So in the end delta G standard and the equilibrium constant K are simply two ways of saying the very same thing.
दो Gibbs quantities काग़ज़ पर लगभग एक जैसी दिखती हैं, और exams उन्हें उलझाने वाले students को सज़ा देते हैं, तो इन्हें साफ़ अलग कर लेते हैं।
Delta G, बिना degree sign के, current composition पर landscape का slope है।
इसका sign बताता है कि ball अभी किस तरफ़ लुढ़केगा: negative मतलब forward, positive मतलब backward, और zero मतलब आप सबसे नीचे, equilibrium पर हैं।
Delta G standard, छोटे degree sign के साथ, बिलकुल अलग चीज़ है: यह किसी given temperature पर reaction का एक fixed number है।
यह वो Gibbs change है जब सब कुछ अपने standard state में हो, और इसका काम है valley को locate करना और K की value fix करना।
यह फ़र्क़ इसलिए ज़रूरी है क्योंकि सिर्फ़ delta G standard, कभी plain delta G नहीं, minus R T ln K relation में जाता है।
बड़ी negative standard value देती है K greater than one, और बड़ी positive standard value देती है K much less than one।
तो आख़िर में delta G standard और equilibrium constant K एक ही बात कहने के दो तरीक़े हैं।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: One story in two languages: Q-vs-K and the sign of ΔG

board_events.text: The direction rule, now with a reason behind it
Subtract the two boxed relations and a single tidy result appears.
If Q is less than K, the ratio is below one, its log is negative, so delta G is negative.
$Q \lt K \Rightarrow \Delta G \lt 0 \Rightarrow$ forward.
If Q is greater than K, the log is positive, delta G is positive, and the reaction runs backward.
This is exactly the Q-versus-K rule from Sub-01, now carrying a thermodynamic reason.
The Q-vs-K test and the sign of delta G are the same statement in two languages.

segments.text: The direction rule from the previous subtopic and the sign of delta G turn out to be the same idea, so let us show why.
Take the two master relations, delta G equals delta G standard plus R T ln Q, and delta G standard equals minus R T ln K, and subtract them.
What drops out is beautifully compact: delta G equals R T times the natural log of Q over K.
Now read it. If Q is less than K, then Q over K is below one, its logarithm is negative, so delta G comes out negative.
A negative delta G means the reaction runs forward, exactly matching the Q less than K rule.
If instead Q is greater than K, the logarithm is positive, delta G is positive, and the reaction runs backward.
This is precisely the Q versus K direction rule you already met earlier, but now it carries a genuine thermodynamic reason underneath it.
So the Q versus K test and the sign of delta G are not two facts to memorise; they are one statement told in two languages.
पिछले subtopic वाला direction rule और delta G का sign दरअसल एक ही idea निकलते हैं, तो चलिए दिखाते हैं क्यों।
दो master relations लीजिए, delta G equals delta G standard plus R T ln Q, और delta G standard equals minus R T ln K, और इन्हें subtract कीजिए।
जो निकलता है वो बहुत compact है: delta G बराबर R T into natural log of Q over K।
अब इसे पढ़िए। अगर Q, K से छोटा है, तो Q over K one से कम है, इसका logarithm negative है, इसलिए delta G negative निकलता है।
Negative delta G का मतलब reaction forward चलती है, जो ठीक Q less than K rule से मेल खाता है।
अगर इसके बदले Q, K से बड़ा है, तो logarithm positive है, delta G positive है, और reaction backward चलती है।
यह बिलकुल वही Q versus K direction rule है जो आप पहले मिल चुके हैं, पर अब इसके नीचे एक असली thermodynamic reason है।
तो Q versus K test और delta G का sign याद करने वाली दो अलग बातें नहीं हैं; ये एक ही statement है, दो भाषाओं में।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Conditions behind ΔG° = −RT ln K

board_events.text: What the relation quietly assumes
The relation uses K expressed through activities, which are dimensionless.
Always feed in the unitless K; never carry concentration units into the logarithm.
It holds only at the temperature for which delta G standard is quoted.
Because of this, both delta G standard and K shift with temperature.
That temperature dependence is the quantitative basis for Le Chatelier's heat effect.
It also assumes ideal behaviour; real concentrated systems need activity corrections.

segments.text: Before we compute with the relation, note the quiet assumptions built into it.
First, the relation uses the equilibrium constant expressed through activities, which are dimensionless quantities.
So you must always feed in the unitless K, and never carry concentration units into the logarithm.
Second, the relation holds only at the specific temperature for which delta G standard is quoted.
The reason sits in the definition, delta G standard equals delta H standard minus T times delta S standard.
Because temperature appears explicitly there, both delta G standard and the constant K shift as the temperature changes.
That very temperature dependence is the quantitative basis for Le Chatelier's heat effect, which you will meet in the next subtopic.
And finally it assumes ideal behaviour, so real systems at high concentration need activity corrections.
Relation से calculate करने से पहले, इसमें छुपी assumptions पर ग़ौर कीजिए।
पहली, relation equilibrium constant को activities के ज़रिए इस्तेमाल करता है, जो dimensionless quantities हैं।
इसलिए हमेशा unitless K डालिए, और concentration units को कभी logarithm में मत ले जाइए।
दूसरी, relation सिर्फ़ उसी temperature पर लागू होता है जिसके लिए delta G standard दिया गया है।
इसकी वजह definition में है, delta G standard equals delta H standard minus T into delta S standard।
चूँकि यहाँ temperature साफ़-साफ़ आता है, इसलिए delta G standard और constant K दोनों temperature बदलने पर shift होते हैं।
यही temperature dependence Le Chatelier के heat effect का quantitative आधार है, जो अगले subtopic में मिलेगा।
और आख़िर में यह ideal behaviour मानता है, इसलिए high concentration वाले real systems को activity corrections चाहिए।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: From ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q to ΔG° = −RT ln K

board_events.text: The master relation and its equilibrium form
At any composition, the Gibbs change is the standard value plus an R T ln Q correction.
At equilibrium the slope is zero and Q has become K, so the left side vanishes.

board_events.latex: 0 = \Delta G^{\circ} + RT\ln K \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta G^{\circ} = -RT\ln K = -2.303\,RT\log K

board_events.text: Solving for K itself gives a compact exponential.
Sign map: negative standard gives $K \gt 1$; zero gives $K = 1$; positive gives $K \lt 1$.

segments.text: Here is the single relation that predicts an entire equilibrium composition from one measured number.
At any composition, the actual Gibbs change equals the standard value plus a correction of R T times the natural log of Q.
So we write delta G equals delta G standard plus R T ln Q.
As the reaction rolls toward the valley floor, Q marches toward K and the slope delta G flattens to zero.
Imposing that equilibrium condition, with delta G zero and Q equal to K, gives delta G standard equals minus R T ln K, or equivalently minus two point three zero three R T log K.
<excited> This is profound: a single quantity you could measure in a calorimeter predicts the whole equilibrium composition without ever running the reaction.
Solving directly for K gives the compact exponential form, K equals e to the power minus delta G standard over R T.
And the sign map falls straight out: a negative standard value gives K greater than one, zero gives K equal to one, and a positive value gives K less than one.
यह वो एकमात्र relation है जो एक measured number से पूरी equilibrium composition की भविष्यवाणी कर देता है।
किसी भी composition पर actual Gibbs change बराबर standard value plus R T into natural log of Q का correction।
तो हम लिखते हैं delta G equals delta G standard plus R T ln Q।
जैसे reaction valley floor की ओर लुढ़कती है, Q, K की ओर बढ़ता है और slope delta G flatten होकर zero हो जाता है।
उस equilibrium condition को लगाने पर, delta G zero और Q बराबर K के साथ, मिलता है delta G standard equals minus R T ln K, या फिर minus two point three zero three R T log K।
<excited> यह गहरी बात है: एक ऐसी quantity जो आप calorimeter में माप सकते हैं, वो reaction चलाए बिना पूरी equilibrium composition बता देती है।
सीधे K के लिए solve करने पर compact exponential form मिलता है, K equals e to the power minus delta G standard over R T।
और sign map सीधे निकलता है: negative standard value देती है K greater than one, zero देती है K बराबर one, और positive value देती है K less than one।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Temperature dependence: van't Hoff and the ΔH°, ΔS° split

board_events.text: How K changes with temperature
Combine the two standard relations to split ln K into enthalpy and entropy parts.
Comparing K at two temperatures cancels the entropy term and gives the van't Hoff equation.
Use $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, T in kelvin, energies in joules per mole.
K rising as temperature rises signals an endothermic forward reaction.
K, Q and ln K are all dimensionless.

segments.text: To see how the constant responds to heating, split it into an enthalpy piece and an entropy piece.
Combining delta G standard equals minus R T ln K with delta G standard equals delta H standard minus T delta S standard does exactly that.
The result is ln K equals minus delta H standard over R T, plus delta S standard over R.
Now compare the constant at two temperatures; the entropy term is temperature-free, so it cancels, leaving the van't Hoff equation.
That reads ln of K two over K one equals minus delta H standard over R, times the quantity one over T two minus one over T one.
For the numbers, use R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole per kelvin, temperature in kelvin, and energies in joules per mole.
The physical reading is direct: if K rises as temperature rises, the forward reaction must be endothermic.
And keep in mind that K, Q and ln K are all dimensionless quantities.
Constant heating पर कैसे react करता है यह देखने के लिए इसे एक enthalpy हिस्से और एक entropy हिस्से में बाँटिए।
delta G standard equals minus R T ln K को delta G standard equals delta H standard minus T delta S standard के साथ जोड़ने पर ठीक यही होता है।
नतीजा है ln K equals minus delta H standard over R T, plus delta S standard over R।
अब constant की दो temperatures पर तुलना कीजिए; entropy term temperature-free है, इसलिए cancel हो जाता है, और van't Hoff equation बचता है।
वो है ln of K two over K one बराबर minus delta H standard over R, into one over T two minus one over T one।
Numbers के लिए R बराबर eight point three one four joules per mole per kelvin, temperature kelvin में, और energies joules per mole में लीजिए।
Physical मतलब सीधा है: अगर temperature बढ़ने पर K बढ़े, तो forward reaction endothermic होनी चाहिए।
और याद रखिए K, Q और ln K तीनों dimensionless quantities हैं।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Worked example — from ΔG° to K (CBSE)

board_events.text: Compute K from a standard Gibbs change
At 298 K, delta G standard equals minus 11.4 kilojoules per mole.
First convert to joules: minus 11400 joules per mole.
Exponentiate to recover K itself.
Negative standard value gives K greater than one: products favoured, as promised.

segments.text: This Board-level example just runs the standard-Gibbs-to-K conversion cleanly.
At two hundred ninety eight kelvin, the standard Gibbs change is minus eleven point four kilojoules per mole.
The first move, and the one students forget, is to convert to joules, giving minus eleven thousand four hundred joules per mole.
Then ln K equals minus delta G standard over R T, which is eleven thousand four hundred over eight point three one four times two hundred ninety eight, and that works out to four point six zero.
Now exponentiate to recover K itself.
K equals e to the power four point six zero, which is approximately one hundred.
And the sign map checks out: a negative standard value has given K greater than one, meaning products are favoured, exactly as promised.
यह Board-level example बस standard-Gibbs-to-K conversion को साफ़-साफ़ चलाता है।
Two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर standard Gibbs change है minus eleven point four kilojoules per mole।
पहला क़दम, जो students भूल जाते हैं, joules में convert करना है, जिससे मिलता है minus eleven thousand four hundred joules per mole।
फिर ln K बराबर minus delta G standard over R T, यानी eleven thousand four hundred over eight point three one four into two hundred ninety eight, और यह निकलता है four point six zero।
अब K निकालने के लिए exponentiate कीजिए।
K बराबर e to the power four point six zero, जो लगभग one hundred है।
और sign map सही बैठता है: negative standard value ने K को one से बड़ा दिया है, यानी products favoured हैं, ठीक जैसा वादा था।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Worked example — ranking K by the sign of ΔG° (NEET)

board_events.text: Rank three reactions without exponentiating
Reaction P has standard Gibbs plus 20, Q has zero, R has minus 20 kilojoules per mole.
The trap: students start exponentiating all three.
Don't. The sign alone orders them, since more negative standard Gibbs means larger K.
So increasing K runs P, then Q, then R.
Delta-G-standard sign instantly places K relative to one; compute only if forced.

segments.text: This N E E T trap rewards you for reading signs instead of reaching for a calculator.
Three reactions are given: reaction P with standard Gibbs plus twenty, reaction Q with zero, and reaction R with minus twenty kilojoules per mole.
The trap is to start exponentiating all three values to find the constants.
Do not; the sign alone orders them, because a more negative standard Gibbs change always means a larger K.
So reaction P, being positive, has K less than one; reaction Q, being zero, has K equal to one; and reaction R, being negative, has K greater than one.
Therefore in order of increasing K it runs P first, then Q, then R.
The speed cue is simple: the sign of the standard Gibbs change instantly places K relative to one, so compute the actual number only if the question forces you to.
यह N E E T trap आपको calculator पकड़ने की जगह signs पढ़ने का इनाम देता है।
तीन reactions दी हैं: reaction P standard Gibbs plus twenty के साथ, reaction Q zero के साथ, और reaction R minus twenty kilojoules per mole के साथ।
Trap यह है कि constants निकालने के लिए तीनों values को exponentiate करने लगें।
मत कीजिए; sign अकेला इन्हें order कर देता है, क्योंकि ज़्यादा negative standard Gibbs change का मतलब हमेशा बड़ा K होता है।
तो reaction P, positive होने से, K less than one; reaction Q, zero होने से, K बराबर one; और reaction R, negative होने से, K greater than one।
इसलिए बढ़ते K के क्रम में यह चलता है पहले P, फिर Q, फिर R।
Speed cue आसान है: standard Gibbs change का sign तुरंत K को one के मुक़ाबले रख देता है, इसलिए असली number तभी निकालिए जब सवाल मजबूर करे।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Worked example — from K to ΔG° (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Exploit log 10 equals one
A reaction has K equal to 10 at 300 K; find its standard Gibbs change.
Use the base-ten form so that log 10 becomes exactly one.
A modest negative value for a tenfold preference toward products.
Note how the logarithm compresses the whole scale.

segments.text: This J E E Main example is a one-line calculation if you pick the right form.
A reaction has K equal to ten at three hundred kelvin, and we want its standard Gibbs change.
Use the base-ten form of the relation, because then log ten becomes exactly one and the arithmetic collapses.
So delta G standard equals minus two point three zero three times R T times log K, which is minus two point three zero three times eight point three one four times three hundred times one.
That evaluates to about minus five thousand seven hundred forty four joules per mole, or roughly minus five point seven four kilojoules per mole.
It is a surprisingly modest negative value for a full tenfold preference toward products.
And that is the takeaway: the logarithm compresses the whole scale, so even a tenfold shift in K needs only a few kilojoules of standard Gibbs change.
यह J E E Main example सही form चुनने पर एक line का calculation है।
एक reaction का K बराबर ten है three hundred kelvin पर, और हमें उसका standard Gibbs change चाहिए।
Relation का base-ten form इस्तेमाल कीजिए, क्योंकि तब log ten ठीक one बन जाता है और arithmetic सिमट जाता है।
तो delta G standard बराबर minus two point three zero three into R T into log K, यानी minus two point three zero three into eight point three one four into three hundred into one।
यह निकलता है लगभग minus five thousand seven hundred forty four joules per mole, या क़रीब minus five point seven four kilojoules per mole।
Products की ओर पूरे tenfold preference के लिए यह हैरान करने वाली modest negative value है।
और यही सीख है: logarithm पूरे scale को compress कर देता है, इसलिए K में tenfold shift के लिए भी सिर्फ़ कुछ kilojoules standard Gibbs change चाहिए।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Worked example — van't Hoff, finding ΔH° (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Get the enthalpy from K at two temperatures
K one is 1.0 times ten to the minus four at 300 K; K two is 1.0 times ten to the minus three at 320 K.
K rises with temperature, which already signals an endothermic forward reaction.
Ln of K two over K one is ln ten, that is 2.303; and one over 300 minus one over 320 is 2.08 times ten to the minus four.
The positive sign confirms the endothermic forward reaction, consistent with K rising on heating.

segments.text: This Advanced example extracts the reaction enthalpy from just two measurements of K.
K one is one point zero times ten to the minus four at three hundred kelvin, and K two is one point zero times ten to the minus three at three hundred twenty kelvin.
Straight away, notice K rises as temperature rises, which already signals an endothermic forward reaction, a preview of Le Chatelier.

Now quantify it with van't Hoff. The log of K two over K one is the log of ten, which is two point three zero three, and one over three hundred minus one over three hundred twenty is two point zero eight times ten to the minus four per kelvin.

Rearranging van't Hoff, delta H standard equals R times that log, divided by the reciprocal-temperature difference, which is eight point three one four times two point three zero three over two point zero eight times ten to the minus four.
That comes out to about plus ninety two kilojoules per mole.
The positive sign confirms the endothermic forward reaction, fully consistent with the constant increasing on heating.
यह Advanced example सिर्फ़ K के दो measurements से reaction enthalpy निकाल लेता है।
K one है one point zero times ten to the minus four, three hundred kelvin पर, और K two है one point zero times ten to the minus three, three hundred twenty kelvin पर।
तुरंत ध्यान दीजिए, temperature बढ़ने पर K बढ़ता है, जो पहले ही endothermic forward reaction का संकेत देता है, Le Chatelier की एक झलक।

अब इसे van't Hoff से quantify कीजिए। K two over K one का log है ten का log, यानी two point three zero three, और one over three hundred minus one over three hundred twenty है two point zero eight times ten to the minus four per kelvin।

Van't Hoff को rearrange करने पर delta H standard बराबर R into वो log, divided by reciprocal-temperature difference, यानी eight point three one four into two point three zero three over two point zero eight times ten to the minus four।
यह निकलता है लगभग plus ninety two kilojoules per mole।
Positive sign endothermic forward reaction की पुष्टि करता है, जो heating पर constant बढ़ने से पूरी तरह मेल खाता है।

sections.subtopic: Equilibrium Constant, Reaction Quotient & Gibbs Energy
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for Gibbs energy and K

board_events.text: Sign and unit traps to avoid
Convert kilojoules to joules before dividing by R, or you inflate the answer by a thousand.
Confusing delta G with delta G standard: only the standard value goes into minus R T ln K.
K equals e to the minus delta G standard over R T is always positive; a negative K means a sign error.
Never mix ln and log; use minus R T ln K or minus 2.303 R T log K, never minus R T log K.
Pro-tip: read the sign of delta G standard first and place K relative to one before any arithmetic.
K up with T means endothermic; K down with T means exothermic.

segments.text: Let us close Gibbs energy with the sign and unit traps that cost the most marks.
First, always convert kilojoules to joules before dividing by R, because R is in joules; mixing them inflates the answer by a factor of a thousand.
Second, never confuse plain delta G with delta G standard; only the standard value goes into the minus R T ln K relation, while the plain delta G governs the current direction.
Third, remember that K equals e to the power minus delta G standard over R T is always positive, so if you ever report a negative K you have made a sign error.
Fourth, never mix natural log and base-ten log; use minus R T ln K, or minus two point three zero three R T log K, but never minus R T log K.
Now the pro-tip: read the sign of delta G standard first and place K relative to one before doing any arithmetic at all.
<whisper> And for temperature problems, lock in one line: K up with temperature means endothermic, K down with temperature means exothermic.
चलिए Gibbs energy को उन sign और unit traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो सबसे ज़्यादा marks खाते हैं।
पहली, R से divide करने से पहले हमेशा kilojoules को joules में बदलिए, क्योंकि R joules में है; इन्हें mix करने से answer हज़ार गुना बढ़ जाता है।
दूसरी, plain delta G को delta G standard से कभी मत उलझाइए; सिर्फ़ standard value minus R T ln K relation में जाती है, जबकि plain delta G current direction तय करता है।
तीसरी, याद रखिए K equals e to the power minus delta G standard over R T हमेशा positive है, इसलिए अगर आप कभी negative K लिखें तो sign की ग़लती हुई है।
चौथी, natural log और base-ten log कभी मत mix कीजिए; minus R T ln K, या minus two point three zero three R T log K इस्तेमाल कीजिए, पर कभी minus R T log K नहीं।
अब pro-tip: कोई भी arithmetic करने से पहले delta G standard का sign पढ़िए और K को one के मुक़ाबले रख दीजिए।
<whisper> और temperature problems के लिए एक line पक्की कर लीजिए: K up with temperature मतलब endothermic, K down with temperature मतलब exothermic।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Le Chatelier: the system fights the change

board_events.text: A disturbed equilibrium pushes back
Le Chatelier's principle: disturb a system at equilibrium and it shifts to counteract the change.
Picture a vegetable mandi at price equilibrium.
Flood it with extra tomatoes (add a reactant) and the system consumes them: prices drop, more get bought — shift forward.
Pull tomatoes off the shelves (remove a product) and the system replaces them — shift forward again.
Squeeze everyone into a smaller stall (raise the pressure) and the crowd rearranges to take up less room.
Equilibrium never prevents the disturbance; it just leans against it.
That single 'counteract the change' rule is the whole of this subtopic.

segments.text: A system at equilibrium is balanced, but it is also responsive, and Le Chatelier's principle states that crisply.
If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to counteract that change.
<curious> Picture a vegetable mandi sitting at price equilibrium, and imagine poking it.
Flood the market with extra tomatoes, which is like adding a reactant, and the system responds by consuming them: prices drop, more get bought, and the balance shifts forward.
Now pull tomatoes off the shelves, which is like removing a product, and the system replaces them, shifting forward again.
Squeeze everyone into a smaller stall, which is like raising the pressure, and the crowd rearranges to take up less room.
In every case the equilibrium never actually prevents the disturbance; it simply leans against it, partially undoing it.
And that one rule, counteract the change, is the whole of this subtopic, applied lever by lever.
Equilibrium पर system balanced ज़रूर है, पर responsive भी है, और Le Chatelier's principle इसे बिलकुल साफ़ कहता है।
अगर equilibrium पर किसी system में concentration, pressure, या temperature का change किया जाए, तो equilibrium उस direction में shift होता है जो उस change को counteract करे।
<curious> एक vegetable mandi सोचिए जो price equilibrium पर है, और उसे थोड़ा छेड़िए।
Market में extra tomatoes भर दीजिए, जो reactant add करने जैसा है, तो system उन्हें consume करता है: दाम गिरते हैं, ज़्यादा बिकते हैं, और balance forward shift होता है।
अब shelves से tomatoes हटा लीजिए, जो product हटाने जैसा है, तो system उन्हें replace करता है, फिर से forward shift।
सबको छोटी stall में ठूँस दीजिए, जो pressure बढ़ाने जैसा है, तो भीड़ कम जगह घेरने के लिए फिर से जम जाती है।
हर case में equilibrium disturbance को रोकता कभी नहीं; बस उसके ख़िलाफ़ झुकता है, उसे थोड़ा undo करता है।
और यही एक rule, counteract the change, इस पूरे subtopic की जान है, lever-by-lever लगाया गया।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: The five levers, and the only one that changes K

board_events.text: Position shifts vs the constant
Five levers move the position: concentration, pressure, volume, inert gas, temperature.
A shift changes the amounts of species; it does not change K.
There is one single exception, and it is temperature.
Only heating or cooling actually rewrites the value of K.
Every other lever just moves the system along the same fixed K curve.
Add reactant or remove product: forward. The reverse: backward.
Inert gas at constant volume: no shift. At constant pressure: toward more gas moles.

segments.text: Before the levers, fix the most important distinction in this subtopic: what shifts, and what actually changes.
Five levers can move the position of equilibrium: concentration, pressure, volume, an added inert gas, and temperature.
But be very careful, because a shift only changes the amounts of the species present; it does not change the value of the equilibrium constant K.
There is exactly one exception to that, and it is temperature.
Only heating or cooling actually rewrites the value of K itself.
Every other lever simply slides the system along the same fixed K curve, changing where it sits without changing the constant.
As a quick summary of directions: adding a reactant or removing a product shifts forward, and the reverse shifts backward.
And an inert gas gives no shift at constant volume, but shifts toward the side with more gas moles at constant pressure.
Levers से पहले इस subtopic का सबसे अहम फ़र्क़ पक्का कीजिए: क्या shift होता है, और सच में क्या बदलता है।
पाँच levers equilibrium की position हिला सकते हैं: concentration, pressure, volume, added inert gas, और temperature।
पर बहुत सावधान रहिए, क्योंकि shift सिर्फ़ मौजूद species की मात्रा बदलता है; यह equilibrium constant K की value नहीं बदलता।
इसका ठीक एक exception है, और वो है temperature।
सिर्फ़ heating या cooling ही K की value को सच में rewrite करता है।
बाक़ी हर lever system को उसी fixed K curve पर सरका देता है, position बदलता है पर constant नहीं।
Directions का quick summary: reactant add करना या product हटाना forward shift करता है, और उल्टा backward।
और inert gas constant volume पर कोई shift नहीं देता, पर constant pressure पर ज़्यादा gas moles वाली side की ओर shift करता है।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Concentration: consume, replenish, drive to completion

board_events.text: The chemist's trick for completion
Add more of any species and the system consumes part of it.
Remove a species and the system replenishes it.
Continuously removing a product drives a reversible reaction toward completion.
Each removal nudges Q below K, so the forward reaction restarts.
Adding a pure solid or pure liquid does nothing — its activity is constant.
So a chemist drains off product to reach completion without ever violating equilibrium.

segments.text: The concentration lever is the gentlest and the most practical, so start there.
Add more of any species that appears in the equilibrium, and the system responds by consuming part of it.
Remove some of a species, and the system responds by replenishing it.
This gives a beautiful trick: by continuously removing a product, you can drive a reversible reaction toward completion.
Each time you remove product, you nudge the reaction quotient Q below K, so the forward reaction simply restarts to catch up.
But note carefully that adding a pure solid or a pure liquid does nothing at all, because its activity is fixed and constant.
So a chemist can quietly drain off product to push a reaction to completion, without ever breaking the rules of equilibrium.
Concentration lever सबसे नरम और सबसे practical है, तो यहीं से शुरू करते हैं।
Equilibrium में मौजूद किसी भी species को और add कीजिए, तो system उसका कुछ हिस्सा consume करके जवाब देता है।
किसी species को हटाइए, तो system उसे replenish करके जवाब देता है।
इससे एक ख़ूबसूरत trick मिलती है: product को लगातार हटाते रहकर आप reversible reaction को completion की ओर धकेल सकते हैं।
हर बार product हटाने पर आप reaction quotient Q को K से नीचे धकेलते हैं, इसलिए forward reaction पकड़ बनाने के लिए फिर से चालू हो जाती है।
पर ध्यान से देखिए, pure solid या pure liquid add करने से कुछ नहीं होता, क्योंकि उसकी activity fixed और constant है।
तो chemist चुपचाप product निकालता रहकर reaction को completion तक ले जा सकता है, equilibrium के नियम तोड़े बिना।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Pressure and volume: the side with fewer gas moles wins

board_events.text: Compression crowds the molecules
Raising the pressure crowds the gas molecules together.
The system relieves the crowding by shifting toward whichever side has fewer gas molecules.
Expanding the volume does exactly the reverse.
So high pressure pushes ammonia synthesis forward, from four moles to two.
For hydrogen plus iodine, delta n gas is zero, so pressure does nothing.
Rule: raising pressure favours the smaller mole count; $\Delta n_{\text{gas}}=0$ means no effect.

segments.text: The pressure and volume lever works only through the gases, and only when their mole counts differ across the arrow.
Raising the pressure crowds the gas molecules closer together.
The system relieves that crowding by shifting toward whichever side has fewer gas molecules, since fewer molecules take up less room.
Expanding the volume, which lowers the pressure, does exactly the reverse and favours the side with more molecules.
Take ammonia synthesis, nitrogen plus three hydrogen giving two ammonia, which goes from four moles of gas to two.
So high pressure pushes this reaction forward, from the four-mole side toward the two-mole side.
But for hydrogen plus iodine giving hydrogen iodide, delta n gas is zero, so pressure has no effect on the position at all.
The precise rule: raising pressure favours the side with the smaller mole count, and if delta n gas is zero, pressure cannot shift it.
Pressure और volume lever सिर्फ़ gases के ज़रिए काम करता है, और तभी जब arrow के आर-पार उनके mole counts अलग हों।
Pressure बढ़ाने पर gas molecules एक-दूसरे के और पास आ जाते हैं।
System उस crowding को कम करने के लिए उस side की ओर shift होता है जिसमें कम gas molecules हैं, क्योंकि कम molecules कम जगह घेरते हैं।
Volume बढ़ाना, जो pressure घटाता है, बिलकुल उल्टा करता है और ज़्यादा molecules वाली side को favour करता है।
Ammonia synthesis लीजिए, nitrogen plus three hydrogen से two ammonia, जो four moles gas से two moles पर जाती है।
तो high pressure इस reaction को forward धकेलता है, four-mole side से two-mole side की ओर।
पर hydrogen plus iodine से hydrogen iodide में delta n gas zero है, इसलिए pressure position पर कोई असर नहीं डालता।
सटीक rule: pressure बढ़ाना कम mole count वाली side को favour करता है, और अगर delta n gas zero हो तो pressure इसे shift नहीं कर सकता।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: The inert-gas trap: constant volume vs constant pressure

board_events.text: The chapter's most common exam trap
At constant volume, adding an inert gas raises total pressure but leaves each reacting gas's partial pressure unchanged.
