board_events.text: Q is unchanged, so at constant volume there is no shift.
At constant pressure, the volume must expand to fit the inert gas.
That expansion dilutes every reacting gas, lowering their partial pressures.
The system then responds exactly as it would to a pressure decrease — shifting toward more gas moles.
This single distinction is the most common exam trap in the chapter.

segments.text: Now the single most tested subtlety in the whole chapter: what an inert gas does.
At constant volume, adding an inert gas raises the total pressure, but it leaves each reacting gas's partial pressure and concentration completely unchanged.
The picture makes it clear: on the left the box stays the same size, so the reacting molecules are just as crowded as before.
Because the partial pressures do not move, the reaction quotient Q is unchanged, and so at constant volume there is no shift whatsoever.
At constant pressure the story flips, because to keep the total pressure fixed while adding the inert gas, the volume must expand.
That expansion dilutes every reacting gas, lowering each of their partial pressures.
So the system responds exactly as it would to a straightforward pressure decrease, shifting toward the side with more gas moles.
<whisper> Lock this in, because this single distinction, constant volume versus constant pressure, is the most common exam trap in the entire chapter.
अब पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली बारीकी: inert gas करता क्या है।
Constant volume पर inert gas add करने से total pressure बढ़ती है, पर हर reacting gas का partial pressure और concentration बिलकुल unchanged रहता है।
तस्वीर इसे साफ़ कर देती है: बाईं तरफ़ box उतना ही बड़ा रहता है, इसलिए reacting molecules पहले जितने ही crowded हैं।
चूँकि partial pressures हिलते नहीं, reaction quotient Q unchanged रहता है, इसलिए constant volume पर कोई shift नहीं होता।
Constant pressure पर कहानी पलट जाती है, क्योंकि inert gas add करते हुए total pressure fixed रखने के लिए volume को फैलना पड़ता है।
वो expansion हर reacting gas को dilute करता है, उन सबके partial pressures घटा देता है।
तो system बिलकुल वैसे react करता है जैसे किसी सीधी pressure decrease पर करता, ज़्यादा gas moles वाली side की ओर shift।
<whisper> इसे पक्का कर लीजिए, क्योंकि यही एक फ़र्क़, constant volume versus constant pressure, पूरे chapter की सबसे common exam trap है।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Temperature: treat heat as a participant

board_events.text: Write heat into the equation
For an exothermic reaction, write reactants in equilibrium with products plus heat.
Adding heat by raising temperature shifts it backward, lowering both yield and K.
For an endothermic reaction, heat is effectively a reactant.
So raising temperature shifts it forward, raising K.
Temperature is the only lever that changes the value of K itself.
Cooling reverses each of these effects.
Memory line: hotter helps the endo.

segments.text: Temperature is the special lever, because it alone changes the constant, and the neatest way to handle it is to write heat into the equation.
For an exothermic reaction, write reactants in equilibrium with products plus heat, treating heat as a product.
Then adding heat by raising the temperature shifts the reaction backward, which lowers both the yield and the value of K.
For an endothermic reaction, heat behaves as a reactant instead.
So raising the temperature there shifts the reaction forward and raises the value of K.
This is the one place where the earlier warning gets its exception: temperature is the only lever that changes the value of K itself.
And cooling simply reverses each of these effects, favouring the exothermic direction.
Keep one memory line handy: hotter helps the endo.
Temperature ख़ास lever है, क्योंकि यही अकेला constant बदलता है, और इसे संभालने का सबसे साफ़ तरीक़ा है heat को equation में लिख देना।
Exothermic reaction के लिए लिखिए reactants का products plus heat के साथ equilibrium, heat को product मानते हुए।
फिर temperature बढ़ाकर heat add करने पर reaction backward shift होती है, जो yield और K की value दोनों घटाती है।
Endothermic reaction के लिए heat बदले में reactant की तरह behave करता है।
तो वहाँ temperature बढ़ाने पर reaction forward shift होती है और K की value बढ़ती है।
यही वो जगह है जहाँ पहले वाली चेतावनी का exception मिलता है: temperature अकेला lever है जो K की value बदलता है।
और cooling बस इन सब effects को उल्टा कर देता है, exothermic direction को favour करते हुए।
एक memory line याद रखिए: hotter helps the endo।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Catalyst: speed, not yield

board_events.text: A catalyst has no thermodynamic power
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally.
It lets equilibrium arrive faster.
It moves neither the position of equilibrium nor the constant K.
So a catalyst cannot improve the equilibrium yield — only the speed of reaching it.
Crediting a catalyst with raising yield or K is a classic exam error.
In any 'maximise yield' problem, the catalyst is a distractor, not a lever.

segments.text: The last qualitative lever is the catalyst, and its role is often overstated, so let us be precise.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction and the reverse reaction by exactly the same amount.
Because it speeds both directions equally, it simply lets the system reach equilibrium faster.
Crucially, it moves neither the position of equilibrium nor the value of the constant K.
So a catalyst cannot improve the equilibrium yield at all; it can only improve the speed of reaching that same yield.
Crediting a catalyst with raising the yield or raising K is a classic and costly exam error.
So in any question that asks you to maximise yield, treat the catalyst as a distractor rather than a genuine lever.
आख़िरी qualitative lever catalyst है, और इसका role अक्सर बढ़ा-चढ़ाकर बताया जाता है, तो सटीक रहते हैं।
Catalyst forward reaction और reverse reaction दोनों की activation energy को बिलकुल बराबर मात्रा में घटाता है।
चूँकि यह दोनों directions को बराबर तेज़ करता है, यह बस system को equilibrium तक जल्दी पहुँचा देता है।
सबसे ख़ास, यह न equilibrium की position हिलाता है न constant K की value।
तो catalyst equilibrium yield को बिलकुल नहीं बढ़ा सकता; यह सिर्फ़ उसी yield तक पहुँचने की speed बढ़ा सकता है।
Catalyst को yield या K बढ़ाने का श्रेय देना एक classic और महँगी exam ग़लती है।
तो जिस भी सवाल में yield maximise करना हो, catalyst को असली lever नहीं, distractor मानिए।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Industry in action: the Haber and Contact processes

board_events.text: Where Le Chatelier earns its money
Ammonia synthesis is exothermic and cuts gas moles from four to two, so yield loves high pressure and low temperature.
Haber in practice: about 200 atm, about 700 K, an iron catalyst, and continuous removal of ammonia.
The temperature is a compromise: low temperature maximises yield but makes the reaction unworkably slow.
The Contact process is also exothermic with fewer product moles, three to two, favoured by high pressure and low temperature.
Contact in practice: moderate pressure near 1 to 2 atm, about 720 K, a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, and excess air.

segments.text: Now watch Le Chatelier pay off in real industry, in the two processes exams love.
First the Haber process: nitrogen plus three hydrogen in equilibrium with two ammonia, with a reaction enthalpy of minus ninety two point four kilojoules per mole.
It is exothermic and it cuts the gas moles from four down to two, so the yield of ammonia is favoured by high pressure and by low temperature.
In practice the plant runs at about two hundred atmospheres, about seven hundred kelvin, with a finely divided iron catalyst, and it continuously removes the ammonia by liquefaction.
That temperature is deliberately a compromise: a low temperature would maximise the equilibrium yield, but it makes the reaction unworkably slow, so a moderate temperature buys a usable rate.
Now the Contact process: two sulphur dioxide plus oxygen in equilibrium with two sulphur trioxide, with a reaction enthalpy of minus one hundred ninety seven kilojoules per mole.
It too is exothermic with fewer product gas moles, three going to two, so again high pressure and low temperature are favoured.
In practice it runs at a moderate pressure near one to two atmospheres, about seven hundred twenty kelvin, over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, with excess air to push sulphur trioxide formation.
अब देखिए Le Chatelier असली industry में कैसे रंग लाता है, उन दो processes में जिन्हें exams पसंद करते हैं।
पहले Haber process: nitrogen plus three hydrogen का two ammonia के साथ equilibrium, reaction enthalpy minus ninety two point four kilojoules per mole के साथ।
यह exothermic है और gas moles को four से घटाकर two कर देती है, इसलिए ammonia का yield high pressure और low temperature से favour होता है।
व्यवहार में plant चलता है लगभग two hundred atmospheres, लगभग seven hundred kelvin पर, finely divided iron catalyst के साथ, और ammonia को liquefaction से लगातार हटाया जाता है।
वो temperature जान-बूझकर एक compromise है: low temperature equilibrium yield maximise करता, पर reaction को नाक़ाबिल-ए-अमल धीमा कर देता, इसलिए moderate temperature एक usable rate ख़रीद लेता है।
अब Contact process: two sulphur dioxide plus oxygen का two sulphur trioxide के साथ equilibrium, reaction enthalpy minus one hundred ninety seven kilojoules per mole के साथ।
यह भी exothermic है और product gas moles कम हैं, three से two, इसलिए फिर high pressure और low temperature favoured हैं।
व्यवहार में यह चलता है moderate pressure लगभग one to two atmospheres, लगभग seven hundred twenty kelvin पर, vanadium pentoxide catalyst के ऊपर, sulphur trioxide बनाने के लिए excess air के साथ।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Putting numbers on the levers: Δn_gas and the α–P relation

board_events.text: The quantitative side of the levers
Pressure acts through the change in gas moles across the arrow.
Raising pressure favours the smaller mole count; if $\Delta n_{\text{gas}}=0$, no positional effect.
For a single-reactant dissociation, reuse the relation from the first subtopic.
Because K p is fixed at constant temperature, raising P makes the denominator grow, so alpha falls.

segments.text: Most of Le Chatelier is qualitative, but two quantitative handles make it exam-ready.
First, pressure acts entirely through the change in the number of gas moles across the arrow.
For a gas reaction a A giving b B, define delta n gas as b minus a.
Then raising the pressure favours the side with the smaller mole count, and if delta n gas is zero there is no positional effect at all.
Second, for a single-reactant dissociation you can reuse the relation we derived in the first subtopic.
That relation, K p equals alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared, rearranges to alpha equals the square root of K p over the quantity P plus K p.
Since K p is fixed at constant temperature, raising the pressure P makes the denominator grow, so the degree of dissociation alpha falls, exactly as Le Chatelier predicts.
Le Chatelier ज़्यादातर qualitative है, पर दो quantitative handles इसे exam-ready बना देते हैं।
पहला, pressure पूरी तरह arrow के आर-पार gas moles की संख्या के change के ज़रिए काम करता है।
Gas reaction a A से b B के लिए delta n gas को b minus a मानिए।
फिर pressure बढ़ाना कम mole count वाली side को favour करता है, और अगर delta n gas zero हो तो position पर कोई असर नहीं।
दूसरा, single-reactant dissociation के लिए आप पहले subtopic में derive की गई relation दोबारा इस्तेमाल कर सकते हैं।
वो relation, K p equals alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared, rearrange होकर बनती है alpha बराबर square root of K p over P plus K p।
चूँकि K p constant temperature पर fixed है, pressure P बढ़ाने पर denominator बढ़ता है, इसलिए degree of dissociation alpha घटता है, ठीक जैसा Le Chatelier कहता है।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Worked example — three disturbances on ammonia synthesis (CBSE)

board_events.text: Predict each shift
Part one, increasing pressure: shift toward fewer gas moles, the product side (two versus four) — forward.
Part two, adding nitrogen: this raises a reactant, so the system consumes it — forward.
Part three, raising temperature: on an exothermic reaction this shifts in the endothermic, reverse direction — backward.
Only in part three does K change; it decreases.
So the three answers are forward, forward, and backward.

segments.text: This Board-level example just applies the levers one at a time to ammonia synthesis.
The reaction is nitrogen plus three hydrogen in equilibrium with two ammonia, and it is exothermic.
Part one, increasing the pressure: the system shifts toward the side with fewer gas moles, which is the product side, two moles against four, so it goes forward.
Part two, adding nitrogen: this raises the concentration of a reactant, so the system consumes it by going forward.
Part three, raising the temperature: on an exothermic reaction, heat is a product, so adding heat shifts it in the endothermic, reverse direction, meaning backward.
And note the key subtlety: only in part three does the constant K actually change, and here it decreases.
So the three answers are, in order, forward, forward, and backward.
यह Board-level example बस levers को एक-एक करके ammonia synthesis पर लगाता है।
Reaction है nitrogen plus three hydrogen का two ammonia के साथ equilibrium, और यह exothermic है।
Part one, pressure बढ़ाना: system कम gas moles वाली side की ओर shift होता है, यानी product side, two moles versus four, तो forward जाता है।
Part two, nitrogen add करना: यह एक reactant का concentration बढ़ाता है, इसलिए system उसे consume करने के लिए forward जाता है।
Part three, temperature बढ़ाना: exothermic reaction में heat एक product है, इसलिए heat add करने पर यह endothermic, reverse direction में shift होता है, यानी backward।
और key बारीकी नोट कीजिए: सिर्फ़ part three में constant K सच में बदलता है, और यहाँ यह घटता है।
तो तीनों answers क्रम में हैं forward, forward, और backward।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Worked example — inert gas on PCl5 dissociation (NEET speed trap)

board_events.text: Constant volume versus constant pressure
The trap: students reflexively say 'more gas, so adding gas shifts it.' Wrong on both counts.
Part a, at constant volume: the partial pressures of all three gases are unchanged, so there is no shift.
Part b, at constant pressure: the system must expand to fit the argon, diluting the reacting gases.
That dilution shifts equilibrium toward more gas moles, the product side — forward, increasing dissociation.
Speed cue: inert gas at constant V is nothing; at constant P it behaves like dilution.

segments.text: This N E E T trap is all about the inert-gas subtlety, so read the fixed condition carefully.
The equilibrium is phosphorus pentachloride gas in equilibrium with phosphorus trichloride gas plus chlorine gas.
The trap is that students reflexively say more gas means adding gas will shift it, and that is wrong on both counts.
Part a, adding argon at constant volume: the partial pressures of phosphorus pentachloride, phosphorus trichloride, and chlorine are all unchanged, so there is no shift.
Part b, adding argon at constant pressure: now the system must expand to make room for the argon, which dilutes the reacting gases.
That dilution shifts the equilibrium toward the side with more gas moles, which is the product side, so it goes forward and dissociation increases.
The speed cue to remember: an inert gas at constant volume does nothing, while at constant pressure it behaves just like dilution.
यह N E E T trap पूरी तरह inert-gas बारीकी पर है, तो fixed condition ध्यान से पढ़िए।
Equilibrium है phosphorus pentachloride gas का phosphorus trichloride gas plus chlorine gas के साथ equilibrium।
Trap यह है कि students reflex में कहते हैं ज़्यादा gas मतलब gas add करने से shift होगा, और यह दोनों तरह से ग़लत है।
Part a, constant volume पर argon add करना: phosphorus pentachloride, phosphorus trichloride, और chlorine तीनों के partial pressures unchanged हैं, इसलिए कोई shift नहीं।
Part b, constant pressure पर argon add करना: अब system को argon के लिए जगह बनाने हेतु फैलना पड़ता है, जो reacting gases को dilute करता है।
वो dilution equilibrium को ज़्यादा gas moles वाली side, यानी product side, की ओर shift करता है, तो यह forward जाता है और dissociation बढ़ता है।
याद रखने वाला speed cue: constant volume पर inert gas कुछ नहीं करता, जबकि constant pressure पर यह बिलकुल dilution जैसा behave करता है।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Worked example — maximising SO3 yield (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Which changes actually raise yield?
High pressure favours fewer gas moles, three going to two, so it increases yield.
High temperature shifts an exothermic reaction backward and lowers K, so it decreases yield.
A catalyst gives faster equilibrium but no change in yield at all.
Excess oxygen adds a reactant and shifts forward, so it increases yield.
Genuine yield boosters are high pressure and excess oxygen; temperature and catalyst only help kinetics.

segments.text: This J E E Main example asks you to separate real yield levers from imposters for the Contact-process reaction.
The reaction is two sulphur dioxide plus oxygen in equilibrium with two sulphur trioxide, and it is exothermic.
High pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, three going to two, so it does increase the yield.
High temperature shifts this exothermic reaction backward and lowers K, so it actually decreases the yield, and is used only to gain rate.
A catalyst gives faster equilibrium but no change in the yield whatsoever.
Excess oxygen adds a reactant, so the system shifts forward, and that increases the yield.
So the genuine yield boosters here are high pressure and excess oxygen, while temperature and catalyst only help the kinetics.
यह J E E Main example आपसे Contact-process reaction के लिए असली yield levers को नक़ली से अलग करने को कहता है।
Reaction है two sulphur dioxide plus oxygen का two sulphur trioxide के साथ equilibrium, और यह exothermic है।
High pressure कम gas moles वाली side को favour करता है, three से two, इसलिए यह yield बढ़ाता है।
High temperature इस exothermic reaction को backward shift करता है और K घटाता है, इसलिए यह असल में yield घटाता है, और सिर्फ़ rate पाने के लिए इस्तेमाल होता है।
Catalyst equilibrium तेज़ देता है पर yield में कोई बदलाव नहीं।
Excess oxygen एक reactant add करता है, तो system forward shift होता है, और यह yield बढ़ाता है।
तो यहाँ असली yield boosters हैं high pressure और excess oxygen, जबकि temperature और catalyst सिर्फ़ kinetics में मदद करते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Worked example — dissociation falls as pressure rises (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Prove Le Chatelier from the algebra
Because K p depends only on temperature, it is a constant at fixed T.
As P increases with K p held constant, the denominator grows, so alpha decreases.
The algebra confirms the qualitative prediction: compression suppresses dissociation.

segments.text: This Advanced example shows Le Chatelier and the equilibrium expression telling one consistent story.
Start from the dissociation relation, K p equals alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared.
Because K p depends only on temperature, at a fixed temperature it is simply a constant.
Rearranging, alpha squared over one minus alpha squared equals K p over P, which gives alpha squared equals K p over the quantity P plus K p.
Taking the square root, alpha equals the square root of K p over P plus K p.
Now read it: as the pressure P increases while K p is held constant, the denominator P plus K p grows, so alpha decreases.
So the algebra confirms the qualitative prediction exactly: compressing the system suppresses dissociation, shifting toward the side with fewer gas moles.
यह Advanced example दिखाता है कि Le Chatelier और equilibrium expression एक ही consistent कहानी कहते हैं।
Dissociation relation से शुरू कीजिए, K p equals alpha squared P over one minus alpha squared।
चूँकि K p सिर्फ़ temperature पर निर्भर करता है, fixed temperature पर यह बस एक constant है।
Rearrange करने पर alpha squared over one minus alpha squared बराबर K p over P, जिससे मिलता है alpha squared बराबर K p over P plus K p।
Square root लेने पर alpha बराबर square root of K p over P plus K p।
अब पढ़िए: जैसे-जैसे pressure P बढ़ता है और K p constant रहता है, denominator P plus K p बढ़ता है, इसलिए alpha घटता है।
तो algebra qualitative prediction की बिलकुल पुष्टि करता है: system को compress करना dissociation को दबाता है, कम gas moles वाली side की ओर shift करते हुए।

sections.subtopic: Le Chatelier's Principle & Factors Affecting Equilibria
sections.title: Traps and pro-tips for Le Chatelier

board_events.text: The four slips that cost marks
Inert gas: constant volume gives no shift; constant pressure shifts toward more gas moles.
Never credit a catalyst with raising yield or K; it changes only the rate of reaching equilibrium.
Apply a pressure shift only when delta n gas is non-zero; hydrogen plus iodine is pressure-insensitive.
Temperature is the one factor that changes K: up for endothermic, down for exothermic.
Pro-tip: write heat as a product or reactant, then treat a temperature change like a concentration change.
For 'maximise yield' questions, separate genuine yield levers from the rate-only catalyst.

segments.text: Let us close Le Chatelier with the four slips that quietly cost marks.
First, the inert-gas rule: at constant volume there is no shift, while at constant pressure the shift is toward more gas moles.
Second, never credit a catalyst with raising the yield or the constant K, because it changes only the rate of reaching equilibrium.
Third, apply a pressure shift only when delta n gas is non-zero; a reaction like hydrogen plus iodine giving hydrogen iodide is pressure-insensitive in position.
Fourth, remember that temperature is the one factor that does change K, raising it for endothermic reactions and lowering it for exothermic ones.
Now a pro-tip: write heat explicitly as a product or a reactant, and then you can treat any temperature change just like a concentration change.
<whisper> And for maximise-yield questions, always separate the genuine yield levers, pressure, concentration and temperature, from the rate-only catalyst.
चलिए Le Chatelier को उन चार slips के साथ बंद करते हैं जो चुपचाप marks खाती हैं।
पहली, inert-gas rule: constant volume पर कोई shift नहीं, जबकि constant pressure पर shift ज़्यादा gas moles की ओर होता है।
दूसरी, catalyst को yield या constant K बढ़ाने का श्रेय कभी मत दीजिए, क्योंकि यह सिर्फ़ equilibrium तक पहुँचने की rate बदलता है।
तीसरी, pressure shift तभी लगाइए जब delta n gas non-zero हो; hydrogen plus iodine से hydrogen iodide जैसी reaction position में pressure-insensitive है।
चौथी, याद रखिए temperature ही वो एक factor है जो K बदलता है, endothermic के लिए बढ़ाता और exothermic के लिए घटाता है।
अब एक pro-tip: heat को साफ़-साफ़ product या reactant लिखिए, फिर आप किसी भी temperature change को concentration change की तरह ट्रीट कर सकते हैं।
<whisper> और maximise-yield सवालों के लिए हमेशा असली yield levers, pressure, concentration और temperature, को rate-only catalyst से अलग रखिए।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Strong versus weak: complete versus partial ionization

board_events.text: Two kinds of train, two kinds of acid
Think of a crowded Mumbai local at peak hour.
A strong acid is the train where every passenger gets off — complete ionization, nobody held back.
A weak acid is the train where only a handful step out — partial ionization, an equilibrium.
So ionic equilibrium is just chemical equilibrium applied to charged species in water.
A weak acid only partially ionizes, so it needs its ionization constant K a.
The rest of this subtopic is the earlier equilibrium machinery, now pointed at ions.

segments.text: Ionic equilibrium sounds new, but it is the same equilibrium logic pointed at charged species, so start with a picture.
Think of a crowded Mumbai local at peak hour, packed to the doors.
A strong acid is like the train where every single passenger gets off at the platform: complete ionization, with nobody held back.
A weak acid is like the train where only a handful step out while the rest stay seated: partial ionization, a genuine equilibrium between those who left and those who stayed.
So the whole of ionic equilibrium is just chemical equilibrium, the ideas from earlier, applied to charged species dissolved in water.
For a strong acid, ionization is effectively complete, so its hydrogen-ion concentration is read straight off the stated concentration.
A weak acid only partially ionizes, so it needs its own ionization constant, written K a.
And the rest of this subtopic is simply that earlier equilibrium machinery, now pointed squarely at ions.
Ionic equilibrium नया लगता है, पर यह वही equilibrium logic है जो charged species पर लगाया गया है, तो एक तस्वीर से शुरू करते हैं।
Peak hour की खचाखच भरी Mumbai local सोचिए, दरवाज़ों तक ठसाठस।
Strong acid उस train जैसा है जहाँ हर एक passenger platform पर उतर जाता है: complete ionization, कोई रुका नहीं।
Weak acid उस train जैसा है जहाँ सिर्फ़ कुछ लोग उतरते हैं और बाक़ी बैठे रहते हैं: partial ionization, उतरे और बैठे लोगों के बीच एक असली equilibrium।
तो पूरा ionic equilibrium बस chemical equilibrium है, पहले वाले ideas, जो पानी में घुले charged species पर लगाए गए हैं।
Strong acid के लिए ionization लगभग पूरी होती है, इसलिए उसका hydrogen-ion concentration सीधे बताई गई concentration से पढ़ लिया जाता है।
Weak acid सिर्फ़ partially ionize होता है, इसलिए उसे अपना ionization constant चाहिए, जिसे K a लिखते हैं।
और इस subtopic का बाक़ी हिस्सा बस वही पुरानी equilibrium machinery है, जो अब सीधे ions पर लगी है।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Three lenses on acid and base: Arrhenius to Lewis

board_events.text: Each definition wider than the last
Arrhenius: an acid releases hydrogen ions in water, a base releases hydroxide ions.
It is simple, but works only in water and cannot explain why ammonia is basic.
Brønsted–Lowry: an acid is a proton donor, a base is a proton acceptor — the workhorse.
Here water acts as the base, accepting a proton; with ammonia it acts as an acid — amphoteric.
Lewis: the widest lens — an acid accepts an electron pair, a base donates one.
Lewis explains why boron trifluoride, with no proton at all, is still an acid.

segments.text: Chemists sharpened the definition of acid and base three times, each lens wider than the last.
The Arrhenius lens says an acid releases hydrogen ions in water and a base releases hydroxide ions.
It is beautifully simple, but it only works in water and cannot explain why ammonia, which has no hydroxide of its own, is basic.
The Brønsted and Lowry lens is the workhorse: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor.
For example, hydrogen chloride plus water in equilibrium with hydronium ion plus chloride ion.
Here water acts as the base, accepting a proton, yet with ammonia water turns into an acid instead, and that dual nature is called amphoteric.
The Lewis lens is the widest of all: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a base is an electron-pair donor.
That is why boron trifluoride, which has no proton at all, still counts as an acid, because it accepts an electron pair.
Chemists ने acid और base की definition तीन बार तराशा, हर lens पिछले से चौड़ा।
Arrhenius lens कहता है acid पानी में hydrogen ions छोड़ता है और base hydroxide ions छोड़ता है।
यह बहुत simple है, पर सिर्फ़ पानी में चलता है और यह नहीं समझा सकता कि ammonia, जिसके पास अपना hydroxide नहीं, basic क्यों है।
Brønsted और Lowry lens workhorse है: acid एक proton donor है और base एक proton acceptor।
मसलन, hydrogen chloride plus water का hydronium ion plus chloride ion के साथ equilibrium।
यहाँ water base की तरह काम करता है, proton लेते हुए, फिर भी ammonia के साथ water acid बन जाता है, और यह dual nature amphoteric कहलाती है।
Lewis lens सबसे चौड़ा है: acid एक electron-pair acceptor है और base एक electron-pair donor।
इसीलिए boron trifluoride, जिसके पास कोई proton ही नहीं, फिर भी acid गिना जाता है, क्योंकि वो electron pair लेता है।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Conjugate pairs and amphoteric water

board_events.text: Partners that differ by one proton
Every acid, on losing its proton, becomes its conjugate base.
Every base, on gaining a proton, becomes its conjugate acid.
Conjugate base means remove one proton; conjugate acid means add one.
A conjugate pair differs by exactly one hydrogen ion, like ammonium and ammonia.
And a deep consequence: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

segments.text: The Brønsted picture comes with a partnership idea that runs through the rest of the chapter.
Every acid, on losing its proton, becomes what we call its conjugate base.
And every base, on gaining a proton, becomes its conjugate acid.
So the simple test is this: to get the conjugate base, remove one proton, and to get the conjugate acid, add one proton.
For instance, the ammonium ion in equilibrium with ammonia plus a hydrogen ion.
A conjugate pair always differs by exactly one hydrogen ion, as with ammonium and ammonia.
And there is a deep quantitative consequence we will use again: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
Brønsted वाली तस्वीर एक partnership idea के साथ आती है जो बाक़ी chapter में चलता रहता है।
हर acid, अपना proton खोकर, वो बन जाता है जिसे हम conjugate base कहते हैं।
और हर base, एक proton पाकर, अपना conjugate acid बन जाता है।
तो आसान test यह है: conjugate base पाने के लिए एक proton हटाइए, और conjugate acid पाने के लिए एक proton जोड़िए।
मसलन, ammonium ion का ammonia plus एक hydrogen ion के साथ equilibrium।
Conjugate pair हमेशा ठीक एक hydrogen ion से अलग होता है, जैसे ammonium और ammonia।
और एक गहरा quantitative नतीजा है जिसे हम फिर इस्तेमाल करेंगे: acid जितना strong, उसका conjugate base उतना ही weak।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Strength is not concentration

board_events.text: Two ideas exams love to blur
Strength asks: of the molecules present, what fraction ionizes?
Concentration asks: how many molecules are there per litre?
A dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid.
Some acids carry more than one ionizable proton — polyprotic acids.
They release those protons one step at a time, never all at once.
Each successive step is far harder, through a quiet reappearance of the common-ion effect.

segments.text: Here is a distinction that exams punish students for blurring, so pin it down now.
Strength asks a fractional question: of the molecules present, what fraction actually ionizes?
Concentration asks a counting question: how many molecules are there per litre?
These are independent, which is why a dilute solution of a strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated solution of a weak acid.
Separately, some acids carry more than one ionizable proton, and these are called polyprotic acids, like carbonic acid, hydrogen sulphide, and phosphoric acid.
They release those protons one step at a time, never all at once.
And each successive step is far harder than the one before, through a quiet reappearance of the common-ion effect, which we will unpack shortly.
यह एक फ़र्क़ है जिसे उलझाने पर exams सज़ा देते हैं, तो इसे अभी पक्का कर लीजिए।
Strength एक fractional सवाल पूछता है: मौजूद molecules में से कितना fraction सच में ionize होता है?
Concentration एक counting सवाल पूछता है: per litre कितने molecules हैं?
ये स्वतंत्र हैं, इसीलिए strong acid का dilute solution weak acid के concentrated solution से ऊँचा pH रख सकता है।
अलग से, कुछ acids एक से ज़्यादा ionizable proton रखते हैं, और इन्हें polyprotic acids कहते हैं, जैसे carbonic acid, hydrogen sulphide, और phosphoric acid।
ये उन protons को एक बार में सब नहीं, बल्कि एक-एक step करके छोड़ते हैं।
और हर अगला step पिछले से बहुत मुश्किल होता है, common-ion effect की एक ख़ामोश वापसी के ज़रिए, जिसे हम जल्दी ही खोलेंगे।

sections.title: Water's self-ionization: the origin of the pH scale

board_events.text: Even pure water carries ions
Even pure water is faintly conducting, because a tiny fraction of molecules swap a proton.
At 298 K this gives hydrogen-ion and hydroxide-ion concentrations each of ten to the minus seven molar.

segments.text: Before any acid or base, water itself sets the stage for the whole pH scale.
Even pure water sits in a faint equilibrium: two water molecules in equilibrium with a hydronium ion plus a hydroxide ion.
That is why even pure water is faintly conducting, because a tiny fraction of its molecules are always swapping a proton.
At two hundred ninety eight kelvin this gives a hydrogen-ion concentration and a hydroxide-ion concentration each equal to ten to the minus seven molar.
The scale you see runs from acidic on the left, through neutral at seven, to basic on the right.
That single number, ten to the minus seven, is the origin of the entire pH scale.
But be careful: the water constant K w equals ten to the minus fourteen only at two hundred ninety eight kelvin, so the neutral value of pH shifts with temperature.
किसी acid या base से पहले, water ख़ुद पूरी pH scale की बुनियाद रखता है।
Pure water भी एक हल्के equilibrium में रहता है: दो water molecules का hydronium ion plus hydroxide ion के साथ equilibrium।
इसीलिए pure water भी हल्का conducting होता है, क्योंकि इसके molecules का एक छोटा fraction हमेशा proton swap करता रहता है।
Two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर इससे hydrogen-ion concentration और hydroxide-ion concentration दोनों ten to the minus seven molar के बराबर मिलते हैं।
जो scale आप देख रहे हैं वो बाएँ acidic से, बीच में neutral seven से होकर, दाएँ basic तक जाती है।
यही एक number, ten to the minus seven, पूरी pH scale की जड़ है।
पर सावधान रहिए: water constant K w बराबर ten to the minus fourteen सिर्फ़ two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर होता है, इसलिए neutral pH की value temperature के साथ shift होती है।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: The common-ion effect and how a buffer resists change

board_events.text: A shared ion suppresses ionization
Add a common ion to a weak-electrolyte equilibrium and Le Chatelier pushes ionization backward.
Pour sodium acetate into acetic acid: the flood of acetate drives ionization to the left, lowering hydrogen-ion concentration.

board_events.text: A solution holding both a weak acid and its salt resists pH change — a buffer.
Add acid and the conjugate base mops it up; add base and the weak acid neutralizes it.
Your own blood is a buffer, holding pH near seven point four.

segments.text: Now a consequence of the common ion that becomes the basis of buffers.
Add a common ion to a weak-electrolyte equilibrium, and Le Chatelier pushes the ionization backward.
For example, pour sodium acetate into acetic acid: the flood of acetate ions drives the ionization to the left, suppressing it and lowering the hydrogen-ion concentration.
The bars make the size of the effect clear: acetic acid alone has a far taller hydrogen-ion bar than the same acid with its salt added.
A solution that holds both a weak acid and its conjugate salt in bulk resists changes in pH, and that is exactly what we call a buffer.
Add some acid and the conjugate base reservoir mops it up; add some base and the weak-acid reservoir neutralizes it.
This is not just a lab curiosity: your own blood is a buffer, the carbonic-acid and bicarbonate system, holding pH near seven point four.
अब common ion का एक नतीजा जो buffers की बुनियाद बन जाता है।
किसी weak-electrolyte equilibrium में common ion add कीजिए, तो Le Chatelier ionization को पीछे धकेलता है।
मसलन, acetic acid में sodium acetate डालिए: acetate ions की बाढ़ ionization को बाईं ओर धकेलती है, उसे दबाते हुए और hydrogen-ion concentration घटाते हुए।
Bars इस effect का साइज़ साफ़ कर देते हैं: अकेले acetic acid का hydrogen-ion bar उसी acid plus salt वाले से कहीं ऊँचा है।
जो solution एक weak acid और उसके conjugate salt को साथ रखता है वो pH के changes को रोकता है, और यही हम buffer कहते हैं।
थोड़ा acid डालिए तो conjugate base का reservoir उसे सोख लेता है; थोड़ा base डालिए तो weak-acid reservoir उसे neutralize कर देता है।
यह सिर्फ़ lab की बात नहीं: आपका अपना ख़ून एक buffer है, carbonic-acid और bicarbonate वाला system, जो pH को seven point four के पास रखता है।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Polyprotic acids: why each step is harder

board_events.text: The constants fall off a cliff
For a polyprotic acid, $K_{a1} \gg K_{a2} \gg K_{a3}$.
First reason: pulling a positive proton off an already-negative ion is electrostatically harder each time.
Second reason: the proton freed in the first step is a common ion for the second, suppressing it.
The common-ion effect operating inside the very same molecule.
The payoff: the pH is governed almost entirely by the first ionization.
So you rarely need K a two or K a three to find a polyprotic acid's pH.

segments.text: Polyprotic acids ionize in stages, and the constants for those stages fall off a cliff.
For a polyprotic acid, K a one is far greater than K a two, which is far greater than K a three.
The first reason is electrostatic: pulling a positively charged proton away from an ion that is already negative is harder at every successive step.
The second reason is the elegant part: the hydrogen ion freed in the first step is itself a common ion for the second equilibrium, so it suppresses that second ionization.
In other words, the common-ion effect is operating inside the very same acid molecule.
The practical payoff for problem-solving is large: because K a one dwarfs the rest, the solution's hydrogen-ion concentration, and hence its pH, is governed almost entirely by the first ionization.
So you rarely need K a two or K a three at all when you just want the pH of a polyprotic acid solution.
Polyprotic acids stages में ionize होते हैं, और उन stages के constants एक cliff से गिरते हैं।
Polyprotic acid के लिए K a one, K a two से बहुत बड़ा है, जो K a three से बहुत बड़ा है।
पहली वजह electrostatic है: एक positively charged proton को पहले से negative ion से खींचना हर अगले step पर मुश्किल होता है।
दूसरी वजह ख़ूबसूरत है: पहले step में छूटा hydrogen ion ख़ुद दूसरे equilibrium के लिए common ion है, इसलिए वो दूसरी ionization को दबा देता है।
दूसरे शब्दों में, common-ion effect उसी एक acid molecule के अंदर काम कर रहा है।
Problem-solving के लिए practical payoff बड़ा है: चूँकि K a one बाक़ी सबसे बहुत बड़ा है, solution का hydrogen-ion concentration, और इसलिए उसका pH, लगभग पूरी तरह पहली ionization से तय होता है।
तो polyprotic acid solution का pH चाहिए हो तो आपको K a two या K a three की ज़रूरत शायद ही पड़े।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: What makes one acid stronger than another

board_events.text: Bond strength and polarity
Acid strength is set by how readily the hydrogen-to-A bond gives up its proton.
Down a group the bond grows longer and weaker, so acidity increases.
$\mathrm{HF} \lt \mathrm{HCl} \lt \mathrm{HBr} \lt \mathrm{HI}$ — bond strength wins over electronegativity.
Across a period, polarity dominates, so acidity rises with the electronegativity of A.
$\mathrm{CH_4} \lt \mathrm{NH_3} \lt \mathrm{H_2O} \lt \mathrm{HF}$.
For oxoacids, more oxygens stabilise the conjugate base, so acidity rises with oxidation state.

segments.text: Finally, what actually makes one acid stronger than another? It comes down to how readily the bond to hydrogen gives up its proton, through bond strength and bond polarity.
Acid strength is set by how easily the hydrogen-to-A bond releases its proton.
Going down a group, that bond grows longer and weaker, so the proton leaves more easily and acidity increases.

So hydrofluoric is weaker than hydrochloric, weaker than hydrobromic, weaker than hydroiodic; hydroiodic acid is the strongest here even though fluorine is the most electronegative, because bond strength wins.
Going across a period, polarity dominates instead, so acidity rises with the electronegativity of the atom A.
So methane is weaker than ammonia, weaker than water, weaker than hydrogen fluoride.
And for oxoacids of the same central atom, more oxygen atoms pull electron density away and stabilise the conjugate base, so acidity rises with the oxidation state, as in the chlorine oxoacid series.
आख़िर में, एक acid दूसरे से strong होता क्यों है? यह इस पर आता है कि hydrogen वाला bond कितनी आसानी से अपना proton छोड़ता है, bond strength और bond polarity के ज़रिए।
Acid strength इस बात से तय होता है कि hydrogen-to-A bond कितनी आसानी से अपना proton छोड़ता है।
Group में नीचे जाने पर वो bond लंबा और कमज़ोर होता जाता है, इसलिए proton आसानी से निकलता है और acidity बढ़ती है।
तो hydrofluoric, hydrochloric से कमज़ोर, hydrobromic से कमज़ोर, hydroiodic से कमज़ोर; hydroiodic acid यहाँ सबसे strong है भले fluorine सबसे electronegative हो, क्योंकि bond strength जीतता है।
Period में आर-पार जाने पर polarity हावी हो जाती है, इसलिए acidity atom A की electronegativity के साथ बढ़ती है।
तो methane, ammonia से कमज़ोर, water से कमज़ोर, hydrogen fluoride से कमज़ोर।

और एक ही central atom के oxoacids में ज़्यादा oxygen atoms electron density खींचकर conjugate base को stabilise करते हैं, इसलिए acidity oxidation state के साथ बढ़ती है, जैसे chlorine के oxoacid series में।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: The water constant, pH and pOH

board_events.text: The scale, defined
Pure water: $[\mathrm{H^+}]=[\mathrm{OH^-}]=10^{-7}$, so pH is seven, neutral.
Add acid and pH falls below seven; add base and pH climbs above seven.
K w carries units of mole squared per litre squared; pH and pOH are dimensionless.

segments.text: Now the formal definitions that turn water's equilibrium into the pH scale.
The ionic product of water is K w equals hydrogen-ion concentration times hydroxide-ion concentration, equal to one point zero times ten to the minus fourteen at two hundred ninety eight kelvin.
The pH is minus the log of the hydrogen-ion concentration, and the pOH is minus the log of the hydroxide-ion concentration.
Taking the log of the water constant links them: pH plus pOH equals fourteen at two hundred ninety eight kelvin.
In pure water the two concentrations are equal at ten to the minus seven, so the pH is seven, which we call neutral.
Add acid and the pH falls below seven, while adding base makes the pH climb above seven.
And note the units: K w carries units of mole squared per litre squared, while pH and pOH are dimensionless.
अब वो formal definitions जो water के equilibrium को pH scale में बदल देती हैं।
Ionic product of water है K w बराबर hydrogen-ion concentration into hydroxide-ion concentration, बराबर one point zero times ten to the minus fourteen, two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर।
pH है minus log of hydrogen-ion concentration, और pOH है minus log of hydroxide-ion concentration।
Water constant का log लेने पर ये जुड़ जाते हैं: pH plus pOH बराबर fourteen, two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर।
Pure water में दोनों concentrations ten to the minus seven पर बराबर हैं, इसलिए pH seven है, जिसे हम neutral कहते हैं।
Acid डालिए तो pH seven से नीचे गिरता है, जबकि base डालने पर pH seven से ऊपर चढ़ता है।
और units नोट कीजिए: K w के units हैं mole squared per litre squared, जबकि pH और pOH dimensionless हैं।

sections.title: Ka, Kb and Ostwald's dilution law

board_events.text: Weak-electrolyte constants
Ostwald's dilution law relates the degree of ionization to the concentration.
Reading: alpha is proportional to one over root c, so dilution raises the degree of ionization.
For a weak base, the mirror gives hydroxide concentration as root K b times c.

segments.text: For weak acids and bases we need their ionization constants and Ostwald's dilution law.
The acid ionization constant K a is hydrogen-ion times conjugate-base over the undissociated acid, and the base constant K b is the mirror, with hydroxide and the conjugate acid.
Ostwald's dilution law relates the degree of ionization alpha to the initial concentration c.
It reads K a equals c alpha squared over one minus alpha, which for a weak acid, where alpha is much less than one, simplifies to just c alpha squared.
That gives alpha equals the square root of K a over c, and the hydrogen-ion concentration equals the square root of K a times c.
The physical reading is striking: alpha is proportional to one over the square root of c, so diluting the acid actually raises its degree of ionization.
And for a weak base the relations are mirror-symmetric, giving the hydroxide concentration as the square root of K b times c, from which you get the pOH and then the pH.
Weak acids और bases के लिए हमें उनके ionization constants और Ostwald's dilution law चाहिए।
Acid ionization constant K a है hydrogen-ion into conjugate-base over undissociated acid, और base constant K b उसका mirror है, hydroxide और conjugate acid के साथ।
Ostwald's dilution law degree of ionization alpha को initial concentration c से जोड़ता है।
यह कहता है K a बराबर c alpha squared over one minus alpha, जो weak acid के लिए, जहाँ alpha one से बहुत कम है, बस c alpha squared बन जाता है।
इससे मिलता है alpha बराबर square root of K a over c, और hydrogen-ion concentration बराबर square root of K a into c।
Physical मतलब चौंकाने वाला है: alpha, one over square root of c के proportional है, इसलिए acid को dilute करना असल में उसका degree of ionization बढ़ा देता है।
और weak base के लिए relations mirror-symmetric हैं, hydroxide concentration देते हुए as square root of K b into c, जिससे आप pOH और फिर pH निकालते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Linking conjugate pairs, and the buffer equation

board_events.text: Two relations you will reuse constantly
Henderson–Hasselbalch gives the pH of a buffer directly from a ratio.
Conjugate conversion: divide, never multiply, to move between K a and K b.

segments.text: Two more relations round out the toolkit, and you will reuse them constantly.
First, for any conjugate pair, the acid constant times the base constant equals the water constant.
Taking logs, that becomes p K a plus p K b equals fourteen at two hundred ninety eight kelvin.
Second, the Henderson and Hasselbalch equation gives the pH of a buffer directly from a simple ratio.
For an acidic buffer, pH equals p K a plus the log of salt over acid.
For a basic buffer, the mirror form gives pOH equals p K b plus the log of salt over base.
And a crucial reminder on the conjugate relation: to move between K a and K b you divide by the water constant, never multiply.
दो और relations toolkit को पूरा करती हैं, और आप इन्हें बार-बार इस्तेमाल करेंगे।
पहली, किसी भी conjugate pair के लिए acid constant into base constant बराबर water constant।
Log लेने पर यह बनता है p K a plus p K b बराबर fourteen, two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर।
दूसरी, Henderson और Hasselbalch equation buffer का pH सीधे एक आसान ratio से देती है।
Acidic buffer के लिए pH बराबर p K a plus log of salt over acid।
Basic buffer के लिए mirror form देता है pOH बराबर p K b plus log of salt over base।
और conjugate relation पर एक ज़रूरी याददाश्त: K a और K b के बीच जाने के लिए water constant से divide कीजिए, कभी multiply नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Worked example — pH of a strong diprotic acid (CBSE)

board_events.text: Do not forget the factor of two
Find the pH of a 0.005 molar sulphuric acid solution, assuming complete dissociation.
Sulphuric acid is a strong diprotic acid: each formula unit gives two protons.
The easy mark to lose here is the stoichiometric factor of two for a diprotic acid.
So the answer is a pH of two point zero.

segments.text: This Board-level example is a one-liner, provided you respect the diprotic nature.
We want the pH of a zero point zero zero five molar sulphuric acid solution, assuming complete dissociation.
Sulphuric acid is a strong diprotic acid, which means each formula unit supplies two protons.
So the hydrogen-ion concentration is two times zero point zero zero five, which is zero point zero one zero, or one point zero times ten to the minus two molar.
Then the pH is minus the log of one point zero times ten to the minus two, which is two point zero.
The easy mark to lose here is the stoichiometric factor of two; forgetting it would wrongly give a hydrogen-ion concentration of just zero point zero zero five.
So the final answer is a pH of two point zero.
यह Board-level example एक line का है, बशर्ते आप diprotic nature का ध्यान रखें।
हमें चाहिए zero point zero zero five molar sulphuric acid solution का pH, complete dissociation मानते हुए।
Sulphuric acid एक strong diprotic acid है, यानी हर formula unit दो protons देता है।
तो hydrogen-ion concentration है two into zero point zero zero five, यानी zero point zero one zero, या one point zero times ten to the minus two molar।
फिर pH है minus log of one point zero times ten to the minus two, यानी two point zero।
यहाँ आसानी से खोने वाला mark है stoichiometric factor of two; इसे भूलना ग़लती से hydrogen-ion concentration सिर्फ़ zero point zero zero five दे देगा।
तो final answer है pH two point zero।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Worked example — the very dilute acid trap (NEET)

board_events.text: An acid can never give a basic pH
Find the pH of a 1.0 times ten to the minus eight molar hydrochloric acid solution.
The trap: writing pH as minus log of ten to the minus eight, giving eight — but pH eight is basic!
At this extreme dilution, the hydrogen ion from water itself, around ten to the minus seven, dominates.
Any acid more dilute than about ten to the minus six molar: include water; the answer sits just under seven.

segments.text: This N E E T trap catches anyone who applies the pH formula blindly.
We want the pH of a one point zero times ten to the minus eight molar hydrochloric acid solution.
The trap is to write pH as minus the log of ten to the minus eight, giving eight; but a pH of eight is basic, and you simply cannot make a solution basic by adding acid.
The flag is that absurd answer. At this extreme dilution, the hydrogen ion supplied by water itself, around ten to the minus seven, actually dominates and cannot be ignored.

Balancing charge together with the water constant gives a quadratic: hydrogen-ion concentration squared, minus ten to the minus eight times the hydrogen-ion concentration, minus ten to the minus fourteen, equals zero, whose solution is one point zero five times ten to the minus seven.
So the pH is minus the log of one point zero five times ten to the minus seven, which is about six point nine eight.
That sits just below seven, faintly acidic, exactly as physical sense demands; and the rule is that any acid more dilute than about ten to the minus six molar must include water's contribution.
यह N E E T trap उन सबको पकड़ता है जो pH formula आँख मूँदकर लगाते हैं।
हमें चाहिए one point zero times ten to the minus eight molar hydrochloric acid solution का pH।
Trap यह है कि pH को minus log of ten to the minus eight लिखकर eight दे दें; पर pH eight basic है, और acid डालकर किसी solution को basic नहीं बनाया जा सकता।
इशारा वही बेतुका answer है। इस extreme dilution पर, water ख़ुद जो hydrogen ion देता है, लगभग ten to the minus seven, वही हावी हो जाता है और नज़रअंदाज़ नहीं किया जा सकता।

Charge balance को water constant के साथ मिलाने पर एक quadratic मिलता है: hydrogen-ion concentration squared, minus ten to the minus eight into hydrogen-ion concentration, minus ten to the minus fourteen, बराबर zero, जिसका हल है one point zero five times ten to the minus seven।
तो pH है minus log of one point zero five times ten to the minus seven, यानी लगभग six point nine eight।
यह seven से ठीक नीचे बैठता है, हल्का acidic, बिलकुल जैसा physical sense माँगता है; और rule यह है कि ten to the minus six molar से ज़्यादा dilute किसी भी acid में water का हिस्सा शामिल करना ज़रूरी है।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Worked example — degree of ionization and pH of acetic acid (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Use Ostwald's approximation
For 0.10 molar acetic acid with K a of 1.8 times ten to the minus five, find alpha, the hydrogen-ion concentration, and the pH.
So alpha is about one point three four percent, comfortably below five percent, so the approximation is valid.
A weak acid gives a mildly acidic pH, well above that of a strong acid at the same concentration.

segments.text: This J E E Main example is the standard weak-acid calculation using Ostwald's approximation.
For zero point one zero molar acetic acid, with K a equal to one point eight times ten to the minus five, we want the degree of ionization alpha, the hydrogen-ion concentration, and the pH.

Since acetic acid is weak, use alpha equals the square root of K a over c, which is the square root of one point eight times ten to the minus four, giving one point three four times ten to the minus two.
So alpha is about one point three four percent, comfortably below five percent, so Ostwald's approximation is valid here.

Then the hydrogen-ion concentration is c times alpha, which is zero point one zero times one point three four times ten to the minus two, giving one point three four times ten to the minus three molar.
And the pH is minus the log of that, which we can write as three minus the log of one point three four, that is three minus zero point one three, giving two point eight seven.
So a weak acid gives a mildly acidic pH of two point eight seven, well above what a strong acid would give at the same concentration.
यह J E E Main example Ostwald's approximation का इस्तेमाल करते हुए standard weak-acid calculation है।
Zero point one zero molar acetic acid के लिए, K a बराबर one point eight times ten to the minus five के साथ, हमें चाहिए degree of ionization alpha, hydrogen-ion concentration, और pH।

चूँकि acetic acid weak है, alpha बराबर square root of K a over c इस्तेमाल कीजिए, जो square root of one point eight times ten to the minus four है, देता है one point three four times ten to the minus two।
तो alpha है लगभग one point three four percent, five percent से आराम से नीचे, इसलिए यहाँ Ostwald's approximation valid है।
फिर hydrogen-ion concentration है c into alpha, यानी zero point one zero into one point three four times ten to the minus two, देता है one point three four times ten to the minus three molar।
और pH है उसका minus log, जिसे हम लिख सकते हैं three minus log of one point three four, यानी three minus zero point one three, देता है two point eight seven।
तो weak acid एक हल्का acidic pH two point eight seven देता है, उससे कहीं ऊपर जो strong acid उसी concentration पर देता।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Worked example — common-ion suppression in a buffer (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Quantify the common-ion effect
To the earlier 0.10 molar acetic acid, add enough sodium acetate to make it 0.10 molar in acetate.
Now compare the hydrogen-ion concentrations, pure acid versus buffer.
The common ion throttled ionization about seventy four-fold, dragging pH up from 2.87 to 4.74.

segments.text: This Advanced example turns the common-ion effect into a hard number.
To the earlier zero point one zero molar acetic acid, we add enough sodium acetate to make the solution zero point one zero molar in acetate, so it becomes a buffer.
By Henderson and Hasselbalch, with salt and acid both at zero point one zero molar, the pH equals p K a plus the log of one, which is just p K a.
Now p K a is minus the log of one point eight times ten to the minus five, which is four point seven four, so the pH is four point seven four.
To see the suppression, compare the hydrogen-ion concentrations of the pure acid and the buffer.
That ratio is one point three four times ten to the minus three over one point eight times ten to the minus five, which is about seventy four.

So adding the common ion has throttled acetic acid's ionization roughly seventy four-fold, dragging the pH up from two point eight seven to four point seven four; that is the common-ion effect made fully quantitative.
यह Advanced example common-ion effect को एक ठोस number में बदल देता है।
पहले वाले zero point one zero molar acetic acid में हम इतना sodium acetate डालते हैं कि solution zero point one zero molar in acetate हो जाए, तो यह एक buffer बन जाता है।
Henderson और Hasselbalch से, salt और acid दोनों zero point one zero molar पर, pH बराबर p K a plus log of one, यानी बस p K a।
अब p K a है minus log of one point eight times ten to the minus five, यानी four point seven four, तो pH है four point seven four।
Suppression देखने के लिए pure acid और buffer के hydrogen-ion concentrations की तुलना कीजिए।
वो ratio है one point three four times ten to the minus three over one point eight times ten to the minus five, यानी लगभग seventy four।

तो common ion डालने ने acetic acid की ionization को क़रीब seventy four गुना दबा दिया, pH को two point eight seven से four point seven four तक खींचते हुए; यही common-ion effect पूरी तरह quantitative रूप में है।

sections.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium — Acid-Base Concepts, pH & the Common-Ion Effect
sections.title: Traps and pro-tips for pH and ionization

board_events.text: The four slips, and two habits that save you
Very dilute acids or bases: fold in water's hydrogen ion; the answer settles just under or over seven.
Strong polyprotic acids: keep the stoichiometric factor, so 0.005 molar sulphuric acid gives 0.010 molar hydrogen ion.
If Ostwald's approximation returns alpha above five percent, discard it and solve the quadratic.
Conjugate base means remove one proton, conjugate acid means add one; and for the pair, divide by the water constant.
Pro-tip: for a hydrogen-ion concentration of m times ten to the minus n, use pH equals n minus log m.
Sanity check: acid gives pH under seven, base over seven; dilution nudges toward seven but never across it.

segments.text: Let us close ionic equilibrium with four common slips and two habits that save you every time.
First, for very dilute acids or bases, below about ten to the minus six molar, always fold in water's own hydrogen ion, and the answer settles just under or just over seven.

Second, for strong polyprotic acids, keep the stoichiometric factor, so zero point zero zero five molar sulphuric acid gives zero point zero one zero molar hydrogen ion, not zero point zero zero five.
Third, if Ostwald's approximation returns an alpha above five percent, discard it and solve the full quadratic instead.
Fourth, keep the conjugate rule straight: conjugate base means remove one proton, conjugate acid means add one, and to convert between K a and K b you divide by the water constant.
Now the first habit: for a hydrogen-ion concentration written as m times ten to the minus n, compute the pH in your head as n minus the log of m.
<whisper> And the second habit, a sanity check on every answer: an acid gives a pH under seven, a base gives a pH over seven, and dilution nudges the pH toward seven but never across it.
चलिए ionic equilibrium को चार common slips और दो habits के साथ बंद करते हैं जो हर बार आपको बचाती हैं।
पहली, बहुत dilute acids या bases के लिए, लगभग ten to the minus six molar से नीचे, हमेशा water का अपना hydrogen ion शामिल कीजिए, और answer seven से ठीक नीचे या ठीक ऊपर बैठता है।

दूसरी, strong polyprotic acids के लिए stoichiometric factor रखिए, तो zero point zero zero five molar sulphuric acid देता है zero point zero one zero molar hydrogen ion, न कि zero point zero zero five।
तीसरी, अगर Ostwald's approximation alpha को five percent से ऊपर दे, तो उसे छोड़कर पूरा quadratic हल कीजिए।
चौथी, conjugate rule सीधा रखिए: conjugate base मतलब एक proton हटाना, conjugate acid मतलब एक जोड़ना, और K a तथा K b के बीच बदलने के लिए water constant से divide कीजिए।
अब पहली habit: m times ten to the minus n लिखे hydrogen-ion concentration के लिए pH दिमाग़ में निकालिए as n minus log of m।
<whisper> और दूसरी habit, हर answer पर एक sanity check: acid pH seven से नीचे देता है, base seven से ऊपर, और dilution pH को seven की ओर धकेलता है पर कभी उसके पार नहीं।

sections.title: Three practical questions, and buffers as shock absorbers

board_events.text: Same equilibrium logic, three real jobs
All three ideas here are earlier equilibrium logic pointed at practical questions.
How do I stop a solution's pH from drifting? When does a barely-soluble salt precipitate? Why is baking soda's solution basic?
A buffer is like the suspension on a highway bus: the road throws potholes, yet the passengers barely feel a jolt.

segments.text: This final subtopic reuses everything you built, pointed at three very practical questions.
All three ideas here, buffers, solubility, and hydrolysis, are simply the earlier equilibrium logic aimed at real-world questions.
The three questions are: how do I stop a solution's pH from drifting, when does a so-called insoluble salt actually precipitate, and why is a solution of baking soda basic?
<curious> Take buffers first. A buffer is like the suspension on an Indian highway bus: the road throws potholes at it constantly, yet the passengers, meaning the pH, barely feel a jolt.
The picture makes it vivid: add the same small amount of acid, and a buffer barely shifts its pH, while pure water crashes down by several units.
A buffer resists changes in pH by keeping a large reserve of both a weak acid and its conjugate base side by side.
Add some acid and the conjugate base reservoir mops it up; add some base and the weak-acid reservoir neutralizes it.
This is life-and-death chemistry: your own blood is a buffer, the carbonic-acid and bicarbonate system, holding pH near seven point four.
यह आख़िरी subtopic आपकी बनाई हर चीज़ को दोबारा इस्तेमाल करता है, तीन बहुत practical सवालों पर।
यहाँ के तीनों ideas, buffers, solubility, और hydrolysis, बस पहले वाली equilibrium logic हैं जो असली दुनिया के सवालों पर लगाई गई हैं।
तीन सवाल हैं: किसी solution का pH बहकने से कैसे रोकूँ, तथाकथित insoluble salt सच में कब precipitate होता है, और baking soda का solution basic क्यों है?
<curious> पहले buffers लीजिए। Buffer एक highway bus के suspension जैसा है: सड़क लगातार गड्ढे फेंकती है, फिर भी passengers, यानी pH, को झटका मुश्किल से महसूस होता है।
तस्वीर इसे साफ़ कर देती है: उतना ही थोड़ा acid डालिए, buffer का pH मुश्किल से हिलता है, जबकि pure water कई units नीचे गिर जाता है।
Buffer pH के changes को इस तरह रोकता है कि वो एक weak acid और उसके conjugate base दोनों का बड़ा reserve साथ-साथ रखता है।
थोड़ा acid डालिए तो conjugate base का reservoir उसे सोख लेता है; थोड़ा base डालिए तो weak-acid reservoir उसे neutralize कर देता है।
यह ज़िंदगी-मौत की chemistry है: आपका अपना ख़ून एक buffer है, carbonic-acid और bicarbonate वाला system, जो pH को seven point four के पास रखता है।

sections.subtopic: Buffers, Solubility Product (Ksp) & Salt Hydrolysis
sections.title: Solubility product: 'insoluble' is never truly zero

board_events.text: Even AgCl dissolves a little
Even salts we call insoluble — silver chloride, barium sulphate, calcium fluoride — dissolve a tiny bit.
In a saturated solution, undissolved solid sits in equilibrium with a faint trickle of its ions.
With the pure solid omitted by the heterogeneous rule, this constant is the solubility product K s p.
K s p is the ceiling on how concentrated the ions can get before the salt crashes out.
It carries units of molar raised to the total number of ions in the formula.

segments.text: The second idea overturns a school myth: no salt is ever perfectly insoluble.
Even the salts we casually call insoluble, like silver chloride, barium sulphate, and calcium fluoride, actually dissolve a tiny bit.
In a saturated solution, the undissolved solid sits in equilibrium with a faint trickle of its dissolved ions.
For silver chloride, that is solid silver chloride in equilibrium with silver ion plus chloride ion.
By the heterogeneous rule from the first subtopic the pure solid is omitted, and the equilibrium constant that remains is called the solubility product, K s p.
You can read K s p as the ceiling on how concentrated the ions are allowed to get before the salt starts crashing out of solution.
And it carries units of molar raised to the total number of ions in the formula, so its units depend on the salt's stoichiometry.
दूसरा idea एक school myth को पलट देता है: कोई salt कभी पूरी तरह insoluble नहीं होता।
जिन salts को हम आम तौर पर insoluble कहते हैं, जैसे silver chloride, barium sulphate, और calcium fluoride, वो भी थोड़ा-सा घुलते हैं।
Saturated solution में undissolved solid अपने घुले हुए ions की एक हल्की धार के साथ equilibrium में रहता है।
Silver chloride के लिए, यह है solid silver chloride का silver ion plus chloride ion के साथ equilibrium।
पहले subtopic के heterogeneous rule से pure solid हटा दिया जाता है, और जो equilibrium constant बचता है उसे solubility product, K s p, कहते हैं।
K s p को आप एक ceiling की तरह पढ़ सकते हैं कि ions कितने concentrated हो सकते हैं इससे पहले कि salt solution से बाहर crash करने लगे।
और यह molar raised to formula में कुल ions की संख्या के units रखता है, इसलिए इसके units salt की stoichiometry पर निर्भर करते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Buffers, Solubility Product (Ksp) & Salt Hydrolysis
sections.title: Salt hydrolysis: the solution takes the side of the stronger parent

board_events.text: Salts are not as innocent as they look
A salt is the child of an acid and a base.
If a salt's ion is the conjugate of a weak parent, that ion reacts with water and tips the pH.
The one-liner: the solution takes the side of the stronger parent.
Sodium acetate comes from a weak acid and a strong base, so the strong base wins and the solution is basic.
Ammonium chloride comes from a strong acid and a weak base, so the strong acid wins and the solution is acidic.
Sodium chloride, from two strong parents, is a draw — neutral.

segments.text: The third idea is that many salts are quietly not neutral at all.
Think of a salt as the child of an acid and a base, the two parents that formed it.
If one of the salt's ions is the conjugate of a weak parent, that ion reacts with water and tips the pH away from seven.
The one-liner that settles almost every question is this: the solution takes the side of the stronger parent.
So sodium acetate comes from a weak acid, acetic, and a strong base, sodium hydroxide, and the strong base wins, making its solution basic.
Ammonium chloride comes from a strong acid, hydrochloric, and a weak base, ammonia, so the strong acid wins and its solution is acidic.
And sodium chloride, formed from two strong parents, is a draw, so its solution is neutral.
तीसरा idea यह है कि कई salts चुपचाप बिलकुल neutral नहीं होते।
Salt को एक acid और एक base की संतान समझिए, वो दो parents जिन्होंने इसे बनाया।
अगर salt का कोई एक ion किसी weak parent का conjugate है, तो वो ion पानी से react करके pH को seven से हटा देता है।
जो one-liner लगभग हर सवाल सुलझा देता है वो है: solution stronger parent की side लेता है।
तो sodium acetate एक weak acid, acetic, और एक strong base, sodium hydroxide, से बनता है, और strong base जीतता है, जिससे इसका solution basic होता है।
Ammonium chloride एक strong acid, hydrochloric, और एक weak base, ammonia, से बनता है, इसलिए strong acid जीतता है और इसका solution acidic होता है।
और sodium chloride, दो strong parents से बना, एक draw है, इसलिए इसका solution neutral होता है।

sections.subtopic: Buffers, Solubility Product (Ksp) & Salt Hydrolysis
sections.title: How a buffer holds steady

board_events.text: Two big reservoirs, one steady ratio
In an acetate buffer both the weak acid and its conjugate base are present in bulk.
Add strong acid and the acetate reservoir absorbs it, turning acetate into acetic acid.
Add strong base and the acid reservoir absorbs it, turning acetic acid into acetate.
Because both reservoirs are large, the salt-to-acid ratio changes only slightly, so pH barely moves.
Capacity is greatest when the two are equal — the half-neutralization point where pH equals p K a.
Numerically, adding a little acid to an ammonia buffer moves pH by under a tenth of a unit.
Adding that same acid to pure water would swing the pH by several units.

segments.text: Now the mechanism, because seeing why a buffer holds makes every buffer calculation obvious.
In an acetic-acid and acetate buffer, both the weak acid and its conjugate base are present in large amounts, side by side.
Add a splash of strong acid, and the acetate reservoir absorbs it, converting acetate into acetic acid.
Add a splash of strong base, and the acid reservoir absorbs it, converting acetic acid into acetate.
Because both reservoirs are large, the salt-to-acid ratio changes only slightly, and the Henderson equation then tells us the pH barely moves.
The capacity is greatest when the two are equal, which is the half-neutralization point where the pH equals p K a, giving the most cushion in both directions.
To see the size of it, take an ammonia buffer and add a little strong acid: the pH slips by less than a tenth of a unit.
<excited> Add that very same amount of acid to a litre of pure water instead, and the pH would swing by several units, from seven down toward two.
अब mechanism, क्योंकि यह देखना कि buffer टिकता क्यों है, हर buffer calculation को आसान बना देता है।
Acetic-acid और acetate वाले buffer में weak acid और उसका conjugate base दोनों बड़ी मात्रा में, साथ-साथ मौजूद हैं।
थोड़ा strong acid डालिए, तो acetate reservoir उसे सोख लेता है, acetate को acetic acid में बदलते हुए।
थोड़ा strong base डालिए, तो acid reservoir उसे सोख लेता है, acetic acid को acetate में बदलते हुए।
चूँकि दोनों reservoirs बड़े हैं, salt-to-acid ratio बस थोड़ा बदलता है, और फिर Henderson equation बताता है कि pH मुश्किल से हिलता है।
Capacity सबसे ज़्यादा तब होती है जब दोनों बराबर हों, यानी half-neutralization point जहाँ pH बराबर p K a, दोनों directions में सबसे ज़्यादा cushion देते हुए।
इसका साइज़ देखने के लिए एक ammonia buffer लीजिए और थोड़ा strong acid डालिए: pH एक-दसवें unit से भी कम खिसकता है।
<excited> वही acid अगर एक litre pure water में डालें, तो pH कई units झूल जाता, seven से नीचे two की ओर।

sections.subtopic: Buffers, Solubility Product (Ksp) & Salt Hydrolysis
sections.title: Linking Ksp to molar solubility: why the coefficient enters twice

board_events.text: The stoichiometric coefficient does double duty
For silver chromate, if s moles dissolve per litre, then silver ion is two s and chromate is s.
The coefficient enters twice: once as a multiplier on the concentration, once as the exponent.
Forgetting either is the classic error, and it is why you cannot just take the square root of K s p.
The square root works only for a one-to-one salt like silver chloride.

segments.text: The most error-prone skill in this subtopic is turning a solubility product into an actual solubility.

Take silver chromate: if s moles dissolve per litre, then because each formula unit releases two silver ions and one chromate, the silver-ion concentration is two s and the chromate concentration is s.
The dissolution is solid silver chromate in equilibrium with two silver ion plus chromate ion.
So the solubility product is two s squared times s, which is four s cubed, and therefore s is the cube root of K s p over four.
Notice the crucial point: the stoichiometric coefficient enters twice, once as a multiplier on the concentration, giving the two s, and once as the exponent, giving the square.
Forgetting either one is the classic error, and it is exactly why you cannot simply take the square root of K s p for this salt.
The plain square root works only for a one-to-one salt, like silver chloride, where both ions come in equal measure.
इस subtopic में सबसे ज़्यादा ग़लती वाला काम है solubility product को असली solubility में बदलना।
Silver chromate लीजिए: अगर s moles per litre घुलते हैं, तो चूँकि हर formula unit दो silver ions और एक chromate देता है, silver-ion concentration है two s और chromate concentration है s।
Dissolution है solid silver chromate का two silver ion plus chromate ion के साथ equilibrium।
तो solubility product है two s squared into s, यानी four s cubed, और इसलिए s है cube root of K s p over four।
अहम बात नोट कीजिए: stoichiometric coefficient दो बार आता है, एक बार concentration पर multiplier के रूप में, जो two s देता है, और एक बार exponent के रूप में, जो square देता है।
इनमें से किसी एक को भी भूलना classic ग़लती है, और यही वजह है कि इस salt के लिए आप बस K s p का square root नहीं ले सकते।
सादा square root सिर्फ़ one-to-one salt के लिए चलता है, जैसे silver chloride, जहाँ दोनों ions बराबर मात्रा में आते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Buffers, Solubility Product (Ksp) & Salt Hydrolysis
sections.title: Common-ion effect on solubility

board_events.text: A shared ion makes a salt far less soluble
Add a common ion and solubility plummets, exactly as it suppressed weak-acid ionization earlier.
For silver chloride in a solution already containing chloride, the chloride is fixed by the added salt.
That forces the new solubility s prime far below its pure-water value.
This is why a precipitate is washed with a dilute common-ion solution, not pure water.
Washing with pure water would dissolve away some of the precipitate you are trying to keep.

segments.text: The common-ion effect returns here, now governing how much of a precipitate will dissolve.
Add a common ion, and the solubility plummets, exactly the same Le Chatelier suppression that throttled weak-acid ionization in the previous subtopic.
For silver chloride sitting in a solution that already contains chloride, the chloride concentration is fixed by the added salt, not by the tiny amount from the silver chloride itself.
So the solubility product becomes silver-ion concentration times that fixed chloride, which equals the new solubility s prime times the added chloride concentration.
That relation forces the new solubility s prime far below its pure-water value.
This is precisely why, in the lab, a precipitate is washed with a dilute solution of a common ion rather than with pure water.
Washing with pure water would dissolve away some of the very precipitate you are trying to collect, losing material.
Common-ion effect यहाँ लौटता है, अब यह तय करते हुए कि precipitate का कितना हिस्सा घुलेगा।
Common ion add कीजिए, तो solubility धड़ाम से गिरती है, बिलकुल वही Le Chatelier suppression जिसने पिछले subtopic में weak-acid ionization को दबाया था।
Silver chloride जो पहले से chloride वाले solution में बैठा है, उसका chloride concentration added salt से तय होता है, न कि silver chloride से आने वाली छोटी मात्रा से।
तो solubility product बनता है silver-ion concentration into वो fixed chloride, जो बराबर है new solubility s prime into added chloride concentration।
वो relation new solubility s prime को उसकी pure-water value से बहुत नीचे धकेल देता है।
यही वजह है कि lab में precipitate को pure water की जगह common ion के dilute solution से धोया जाता है।
Pure water से धोने पर उसी precipitate का कुछ हिस्सा घुल जाता, जिसे आप इकट्ठा करना चाहते हैं, और material का नुक़सान होता।

sections.subtopic: Buffers, Solubility Product (Ksp) & Salt Hydrolysis
sections.title: Selective precipitation: the smaller Ksp goes first

board_events.text: Separating ions by controlling one reagent
When one reagent can precipitate two ions, the salt with the smaller K s p saturates first.

board_events.caption: Adding silver ion: silver chloride reaches its threshold long before silver chromate.

board_events.text: It needs less of the added ion to start crashing out.
Adding silver ion slowly, silver chloride begins precipitating at a far lower silver concentration than silver chromate.
So chloride is removed almost completely before the chromate even begins to drop.
This staggering is how qualitative-analysis groups are separated, and the basis of the Mohr titration endpoint.

segments.text: Because different salts have different solubility products, one reagent can pick ions out one at a time.
When one added reagent can precipitate two different ions, the salt with the smaller solubility product reaches saturation first.
The diagram shows it on an axis of silver-ion concentration: silver chloride hits its threshold long before silver chromate.
The reason is simple: the salt with the smaller solubility product needs less of the added ion to start crashing out.
So if you add silver ion slowly to a mixture, silver chloride begins precipitating at a far lower silver concentration than silver chromate does.
As a result, chloride is removed almost completely from the solution before the chromate even begins to drop out.
This staggering is exactly how qualitative-analysis groups are separated, and it is the basis of the red silver-chromate endpoint in a Mohr titration.
चूँकि अलग-अलग salts के solubility products अलग होते हैं, एक reagent ions को एक-एक करके चुन सकता है।
जब एक added reagent दो अलग ions को precipitate कर सके, तो छोटे solubility product वाला salt पहले saturation पर पहुँचता है।
Diagram इसे silver-ion concentration के axis पर दिखाता है: silver chloride अपने threshold पर silver chromate से बहुत पहले पहुँच जाता है।
वजह आसान है: छोटे solubility product वाले salt को crash होना शुरू करने के लिए added ion की कम मात्रा चाहिए।
तो अगर आप किसी mixture में silver ion धीरे-धीरे डालें, silver chloride, silver chromate से बहुत कम silver concentration पर ही precipitate होना शुरू कर देता है।
नतीजा यह कि chromate के गिरना शुरू होने से पहले ही chloride solution से लगभग पूरी तरह निकल जाता है।
यही staggering वो तरीक़ा है जिससे qualitative-analysis groups अलग किए जाते हैं, और यही Mohr titration के red silver-chromate endpoint की बुनियाद है।

segments.text: The buffer toolkit is one main equation plus two rules of thumb.
For an acidic buffer, made of a weak acid and its salt, the pH equals p K a plus the log of salt over acid.
So pH equals p K a plus log of the salt-to-acid ratio.
For a basic buffer, made of a weak base and its salt, the mirror form applies.
There, pOH equals p K b plus the log of salt over base.
Two rules of thumb: maximum buffer capacity is at equal amounts, where the pH equals p K a, and the useful buffering range is roughly p K a plus or minus one.
And a practical shortcut: only the ratio matters, so moles work just as well as molarities, because the volume cancels top and bottom.
Buffer toolkit एक मुख्य equation plus दो rules of thumb है।
Acidic buffer के लिए, जो weak acid और उसके salt से बना है, pH बराबर p K a plus log of salt over acid।
तो pH बराबर p K a plus log of salt-to-acid ratio।
Basic buffer के लिए, जो weak base और उसके salt से बना है, mirror form लागू होता है।
वहाँ pOH बराबर p K b plus log of salt over base।
दो rules of thumb: maximum buffer capacity बराबर मात्रा पर होती है, जहाँ pH बराबर p K a, और useful buffering range लगभग p K a plus or minus one है।
और एक practical shortcut: सिर्फ़ ratio मायने रखता है, इसलिए moles भी molarities जितने ही काम करते हैं, क्योंकि volume ऊपर-नीचे cancel हो जाता है।
